A Sou' Wester - David James c.1897.png.title: A Sou'wester
facts: James specialized almost entirely in crashing waves, working only in oil and earning a reputation as a master of the breaking sea.
'David James' was a working name; the painter was born Joseph Donahue in Ireland in 1853.
He painted realistic 'sea-pieces' from England's south-western coasts after settling in Plymouth in the 1880s.
A sou'wester is both a strong wind from the southwest and the waterproof hat sailors wore against it.

A Broad Valley at Sunset - Hippolyte Pet.title: A Broad Valley at Sunset
facts: Petitjean learned the dot-by-dot technique directly from Georges Seurat, applying color in tiny touches the eye blends at a distance.
He met Seurat in Paris in 1884, and on Seurat's encouragement joined the Neo-Impressionists alongside Paul Signac and Camille Pissarro.
In later years he loosened the strict dots into a freer style of widely spaced spots of pure color, often in watercolor.

Above the Clouds I - Georgia O'Keeffe 19.title: Above the Clouds I
facts: Rows of flat white clouds drift toward the horizon like stepping stones, a view O'Keeffe first saw from an airplane window.
She took up flying late in life and was struck by the endless cloud floor seen from above on her trips around the world.
The painting opens her late cloud-and-sky series, which she pursued into her seventies and eighties.
It is held by the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe.

Abstract - Dora Chapman c. 1970.png.title: Abstract
facts: Chapman was an Australian painter, art teacher and printmaker who lived from 1911 to 1995.
From around 1969 she turned to stylised female portrait heads, exploring human character rather than specific individuals.
Silkscreen printing remained a major interest for her even after she retired from teaching.

Abstract (red) - Dora Chapman 1960.png.title: Abstract (red)
facts: Dora Chapman trained and later taught at the South Australian School of Arts and Crafts in Adelaide.
In 1946 she co-founded the Studio of Realist Art (SORA) in Sydney, a group built around social-realist principles.
She worked across many media over her career, from oils and watercolour to etching and silkscreen printing.

Abstract painting - Frank Hinder 1951.jp.title: Abstract Painting
facts: Hinder was a pioneer of abstract art in Australia, building his compositions on dynamic symmetry, a system of geometric proportion he learned while studying in the United States.
He trained in Chicago and New York in the late 1920s, an unusual choice for an Australian artist when most went to Britain or France.

Abstraction - Vicente do Rego Monteiro 1.title: Abstraction
facts: Rego Monteiro trained in Paris from age twelve, studying at the Academie Julian and exhibiting at the Salon des Independants in 1913 while still a teenager.
He showed work in Sao Paulo's landmark 1922 Modern Art Week, the event widely seen as the birth of Brazilian modernism.
His earlier figures drew on Marajoara art, the ancient ceramic tradition of Marajo Island at the mouth of the Amazon.
A fire in the late 1920s destroyed many of his best paintings, and his work stayed little known in Brazil until the 1960s.
Besides painting he was a poet and publisher, dividing his later years between cafes along the Seine in Paris and the Capibaribe river in his native Recife.

Across the Fields - Édouard Vuillard 189.title: Across the Fields (À travers champs)
facts: Vuillard belonged to the Nabis ('prophets'), who flattened scenes into decorative patches of pattern and color.
This is a color lithograph from 'Landscapes and Interiors,' a portfolio of twelve prints published by dealer Ambroise Vollard.
The figures dissolve into soft blots of color, yet a woman in a striped dress and a man in green stay clearly readable.

Almond Blossom - Vincent van Gogh Februa.title: Almond Blossom
facts: Painted as a gift for his newborn nephew, also named Vincent, to hang over the baby's bed.
The branching style borrows openly from Japanese woodblock prints van Gogh collected.
Almond trees are among the first to bloom each spring, so the blossoms stand for new life and a fresh start.
The family kept it close all their lives, and it remains one of the treasures of the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
He set the pale branches against a flat sheet of turquoise sky, with no horizon, as if looking straight up into the tree.

American Gothic - Grant Wood 1930.jpg.title: American Gothic
facts: The two figures never posed together at the house. Wood used his sister Nan as the woman and his dentist, Dr. Byron McKeeby, as the man, painting each one separately.
Wood spotted the little white farmhouse, with its one Gothic-style pointed window, while driving through Eldon, Iowa, and imagined the kind of people who might live there.
He painted it on beaverboard, a pressed wood panel, rather than canvas, working in a tight, smooth style inspired by the early Flemish painters he admired.
The Art Institute of Chicago awarded it a prize and bought it in 1930, and it has stayed in the collection ever since.
People argued from the start over whether it mocked or honored rural Americans. Wood said he meant it as a respectful portrait of hardworking country folk.
It has been parodied countless times, with the pitchfork-holding pair restaged in cartoons, ads, and posters for nearly a century.

Apollo 12 Splash Down - Alma Thomas 1970.title: Apollo 12 "Splash Down"
facts: The painting belongs to Thomas's Space series, abstractions she made after watching televised coverage of NASA's Apollo missions and moon landings.
Its title refers to the ocean splashdown that ended an Apollo flight, when the capsule parachuted into the sea to be recovered.
Thomas was in her late seventies when she made her Space paintings, decades after retiring from teaching art in Washington schools.
She built the surface from short, mosaic-like dabs of color, a method she used across her late abstract work.
Thomas said the wonders of space exploration set her creativity in motion and that color television let everyone share the thrill.

Apple Trees - Wojciech Weiss 1916.jpg.title: Apple Trees
facts: Weiss was a leading painter of Young Poland, the country's turn-of-the-century modernist movement.
From about 1915 to 1918 he painted often at Kalwaria, turning out sunlit orchards and garden scenes like this one.
His work of these years was driven by a deep admiration for nature and the richness of its color.

At Flushing (À Flessingue) - Paul Signac.title: At Flushing (À Flessingue)
facts: A lifelong sailor, Signac owned dozens of boats and painted Europe's ports from the water; Flushing (Vlissingen) is a Dutch harbor town.
After Seurat died in 1891 at age 31, Signac became the sole leader of Neo-Impressionism and its chief spokesman for the rest of his life.
Signac built his pictures from separate dabs of pure color meant to mix in the viewer's eye, not on the palette, a method called Divisionism.
In 1899 he published a book tracing color from Delacroix to Neo-Impressionism; Matisse and the Fauves read it closely a few years later.

At the Moulin Rouge The Dance - Henri de.title: At the Moulin Rouge: The Dance
facts: The lanky man teaching a dancer is Valentin le Desosse, 'the Boneless,' a star performer at the Moulin Rouge known for his rubbery limbs.
The Moulin Rouge opened in 1889, and this canvas hung on the cabaret's own walls from 1890 to 1893, advertising its nightly spectacle.
Toulouse-Lautrec made the dance hall his great subject, sketching its performers and patrons from a regular table night after night.
The painting now lives at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, part of a collection bequeathed by Henry P. McIlhenny in 1986.

Avant la corrida - Amadeo de Souza Cardo.title: Avant la corrida (Before the Bullfight)
facts: Souza Cardoso showed this canvas at the 1912 Salon d'Automne in Paris, his first time exhibiting at the Grand Palais.
It traveled to New York for the 1913 Armory Show, the exhibition that introduced European modern art to a wide American public.
An American collector bought the picture at the Armory Show, and it then vanished from public view for more than 90 years.
The Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation in Lisbon tracked the painting down and acquired it, returning a long-lost work to Portugal.
The artist split his life between Paris and his family home at Manhufe in northern Portugal, staying close to the avant-garde of his day.

Banks of the Seine at Argenteuil - Édoua.title: Banks of the Seine at Argenteuil
facts: Painted the summer Manet worked side by side with Monet at Argenteuil, the closest he ever came to pure Impressionism.
Argenteuil, a riverside town just downstream from Paris, was a favorite Sunday spot for boating and a magnet for the young Impressionists.
Manet never showed with the Impressionists, preferring the official Salon, yet that summer beside Monet visibly loosened and brightened his touch.

Banks of the Seine, Vétheuil - Claude Mo.title: Banks of the Seine, Vétheuil
facts: Monet moved to the small village of Vétheuil in 1878 and painted the Seine there more than 150 times.
He worked through a period of deep grief here: his first wife, Camille, died at Vétheuil in 1879, the year before this view.
Vétheuil sits on a curve of the Seine northwest of Paris, far smaller and quieter than the suburbs Monet had painted before.
This was Monet's first painting accepted at the official Salon in years, marking a brief return to the establishment he usually avoided.

Beach Scene - Pierre-Auguste Renoir 1883.title: Beach Scene
facts: Around 1883 Renoir entered what he called his 'sour' period, tightening his soft Impressionist touch into firmer, more classical drawing.
A trip to Italy in 1881 and 1882 led Renoir to study Raphael and Pompeian frescoes, pushing his work toward clearer line and form.
Renoir sketched the Normandy coast near Dieppe in these years, then often built finished beach pictures back in the studio.

Big City Cab - Rainer Fetting 1995.jpg.title: Big City Cab
facts: Fetting was a leader of the Neue Wilde, the raw, brightly colored German painting revival of the early 1980s.
He co-founded Berlin's Galerie am Moritzplatz in the late 1970s, a hub for the city's young 'wild' painters.
Living in New York from the 1980s, Fetting often painted the energy of its streets, taxis, and harbor.

Blue and Green Music - Georgia O'Keeffe.title: Blue and Green Music
facts: O'Keeffe was trying to paint music itself, translating sound into shape and color the way a melody might look if you could see it.
She admired the idea, shared by other modernists, that color and form could move a viewer the way music does, without picturing any object.
Sharp and soft edges play against each other to suggest rhythm, with bladelike greens cutting through a deep blue ground.
The painting entered the Art Institute of Chicago through the Alfred Stieglitz Collection; Stieglitz was the photographer and dealer she later married.
O'Keeffe disliked having her abstractions explained, once saying that the things people read into her work were rarely her own.

Blue Line - Georgia O'Keeffe 1919.jpg.title: Blue Line
facts: O'Keeffe painted this the same year she committed fully to painting in New York after years teaching art in Texas and South Carolina.
Two ribbon-like forms rise from a shared base to meet a single vertical blue line, a near-abstract image many read as a pairing of two presences.
The work belongs to a run of abstractions O'Keeffe made by distilling feeling into pure shape and color rather than depicting a scene.
It is held by the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe, the museum devoted entirely to her work.

Blue poles - Jackson Pollock 1952.jpg.title: Blue Poles
facts: Pollock laid the unstretched canvas flat on the floor and dripped, flung, and poured enamel and aluminum house paint across it while moving around all four sides.
It was first shown as 'Number 11, 1952'; Pollock added the title 'Blue Poles' two years later, for the eight dark vertical stripes that cut across the surface.
Australia's government bought the work in 1973 for A$1.3 million, then a record for an American painting, sparking a national controversy over the price.
Now the most-viewed work at the National Gallery of Australia, it has left the country only twice on loan, to New York and London.
Pollock worked in a converted barn studio at his home in Springs, on Long Island, where he developed his floor-based pouring method.

Blue--A - Georgia O'Keeffe 1959.jpg.title: Blue--A
facts: A broad band of blue sweeps from the lower left to the upper right, a spare composition built from light, dark, and one slim stripe.
O'Keeffe painted it at Abiquiu, her adobe home in northern New Mexico, where she lived and worked for decades.
It shows that she kept making pure abstractions late in her career, the same impulse that drove her earliest work in the 1910s.
The painting belongs to the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe.

Boat with Sail (Panormos, Tinos) - Nikos.title: Boat with Sail (Panormos, Tinos)
facts: Lytras painted the harsh Aegean light of his family's island, Tinos, with thick strokes that pushed Greek painting toward Expressionism.
He set the horizon high and ringed it with fishing houses, flattening the scene to keep it on the picture plane rather than receding into deep perspective.
Along with Parthenis and Maleas, Lytras is credited with revitalizing modern Greek art in the early twentieth century.
The painting is held by the National Gallery in Athens.

Botafogo Bay - Nicolau Antônio Facchinet.title: Botafogo Bay
facts: Facchinetti was born in Treviso, Italy, and moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1849, where he became one of Brazil's leading landscape painters.
From 1870 he was encouraged by Princess Isabel, daughter of Emperor Pedro II, and held the title of her household landscape painter.
He painted many panoramas of Rio, setting its new houses against the lush nature surrounding the city.
This view is held by the Museu de Arte de São Paulo (MASP).

Boulevard Montmartre, Spring - Camille P.title: Boulevard Montmartre, Spring
facts: One of fourteen views of the same boulevard Pissarro painted from a hotel window, tracking the street through seasons and times of day.
He worked from the Grand Hotel de Russie, where his high room gave an almost bird's-eye view of carriages, omnibuses, and crowds.
The series included a rare night scene, the only nocturne, now in the National Gallery in London.

Breezing Up (A Fair Wind) - Winslow Home.title: Breezing Up (A Fair Wind)
facts: Homer worked the canvas over three years, beginning it in New York from sketches he had made on the docks of Gloucester, Massachusetts.
The boat is a catboat carrying a man, three boys, and the day's catch through Gloucester harbor under a steady wind.
Homer's first title was simply 'A Fair Wind'; the catchier 'Breezing Up' was added later and stuck.
It has become one of the most beloved images of nineteenth-century American life and now hangs in the National Gallery of Art.

Canal of Overschie - Paul Signac 1906.jp.title: Canal of Overschie
facts: Signac sailed his own boat to Rotterdam in 1906, painting the Dutch canals in mosaic-like squares of color.
Overschie is a village now part of Rotterdam, set along the canals that drain the low Dutch countryside into the river Maas.
By this date Signac's early round dots had widened into broader, brick-like touches that cover the canvas like a tiled mosaic.
Struck by Rotterdam's busy port, he wrote on a postcard: 'From my window! What industriousness! I am enthusiastic, but amazed.'

Carica di lancieri - Umberto Boccioni 19.title: Carica di lancieri (Charge of the Lancers)
facts: This is the only work Boccioni devoted entirely to the theme of war, made as Italy moved toward entering the First World War.
He built it as a collage, gluing scraps of newspaper onto the surface and working over them in tempera, a rare method for him.
Slashing black lines and hard geometric shapes drive the clash of cavalry horses and bayonets into a blur of speed and force.
The collage was reproduced in the art journal La Grande Illustrazione, based in Pescara, in January 1915.
The piece is held in the Museo del Novecento in Milan.

Champs Élysées - Maurice Prendergast c..title: Champs Élysées
facts: Prendergast built scenes from small dabs of bright color, a patchwork effect often described as mosaic-like.
On a 1907 trip to France he was struck by Cezanne and the Fauves, and afterward worked more heavily in oil.
He was born at a family trading post in Newfoundland and grew up in Boston's South End.
An apprenticeship to a commercial artist as a youth trained him in the flat, bright patterning that marks his mature work.
He was one of The Eight, the group whose 1908 New York show challenged the conservative American art establishment.

Chromatastic Paintings in Hospitals - Ia.title: Chromatastic (Paintings in Hospitals)
facts: This print was made to benefit Paintings in Hospitals, a charity that brings art into health and care settings, of which Davenport is a patron.
Davenport has said his own time in hospital felt empty and bleak, which drew him to work that brings colour and energy to patients.
He builds his images by pouring high-gloss paint in long parallel lines so it streams down the surface and pools at the bottom.
He was the youngest artist ever nominated for the Turner Prize, shortlisted in 1991 at age 25.
Davenport studied at Goldsmiths in London alongside Damien Hirst and Gary Hume, and showed in Hirst's landmark 1988 'Freeze' exhibition.

Ciboure - Paul Signac 1929.jpg.title: Ciboure
facts: Ciboure is a Basque fishing village on France's Atlantic coast; in his later years Signac toured the coastline painting its harbors, often in watercolor.
In 1929 the collector Gaston Lévy funded Signac's dream project to paint a hundred French ports; he finished the watercolor series in 1931.
Signac would sketch a harbor on the spot in pencil and watercolor, then sometimes work it up into a larger studio oil later.

Circles - Vicente do Rego Monteiro 1962..title: Circles
facts: Rego Monteiro was born in Recife in 1899 and sent to Paris at age twelve, training at the Academie Julian.
He took part in Sao Paulo's 1922 Modern Art Week, the founding event of modernism in Brazil.
From 1922 he exhibited with Leonce Rosenberg's Galerie de l'Effort Moderne, a leading Paris home for Cubism.
He fused Cubism and Art Deco with the geometry of ancient Marajoara pottery from the Amazon.
He worked as a poet and publisher as well as a painter, and was nearly forgotten in Brazil until rediscovered in the mid-1960s.

Circular Forms, Sun, Moon - Robert Delau.title: Circular Forms, Sun, Moon
facts: The work also goes by the title Simultaneous Contrasts: Sun and Moon, and the canvas at New York's Museum of Modern Art is signed and dated 1912.
Delaunay drew on nineteenth-century color theory, letting glowing discs of red, orange, blue and green stand in for the sun and the moon, day and night.
He arranged the floating circles into two poles: a brilliant solar cluster on one side and concentric, thickly painted rings for the nocturnal side on the other.
Critics consider his Circular Forms the fullest flowering of Orphism, the lyrical, music-like abstraction the poet Guillaume Apollinaire named after the mythical bard Orpheus.

Cliff Walk at Pourville - Claude Monet 1.title: Cliff Walk at Pourville
facts: The two women on the cliff are likely the daughters of Alice Hoschedé, Monet's future wife.
Conservators found Monet scraped out a third figure to open up the view of the sea.
Pourville is a small seaside resort on the Normandy coast near Dieppe, where Monet spent several productive months in 1882.
Wind is everywhere in the picture: the grasses bend, the women's dresses billow, and sailboats lean across the water below.

Cloud Study - John Constable c. 1821.jpg.title: Cloud Study
facts: Constable called his open-air sky sketching 'skying,' making dozens of cloud studies at Hampstead in 1821-22 and noting the weather and time of day on the back of each.

Clouds 5 - Yellow Horizon and Clouds - G.title: Clouds 5 / Yellow Horizon and Clouds
facts: A field of patterned clouds fills most of the canvas, capped by a thin horizon that shades from yellow to green to blue.
The seven-foot-wide painting is part of the cloud series O'Keeffe based on the view from airplane windows.
The aerial sweep here points toward Sky Above Clouds IV, the enormous twenty-four-foot canvas she finished in 1965.
It is held by the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe.

Coffee Table at Lake Starnberg - Wilhelm.title: Coffee Table at Lake Starnberg
facts: Trübner treated everyday subjects with deliberate seriousness, arguing a well-painted table mattered as much as any grand history scene.
Lake Starnberg, just south of Munich, was a popular Bavarian retreat where city dwellers came to boat, swim and take the air.
A teacher as well as a painter, Trübner spent his later years leading the Karlsruhe academy, passing his realist outlook to younger artists.

Color Study, Squares with Concentric Cir.title: Color Study, Squares with Concentric Circles
facts: This is a working study, watercolor and gouache on paper, made to test how colors behave when set side by side.
It survives at the Lenbachhaus in Munich, home to one of the richest collections of Blue Rider works.
Kandinsky saw the circle as a link to the cosmos, the simplest shape carrying the deepest mystery.
Though made only as a private color exercise, it became one of his most widely reproduced images.
The twelve panels are loose and freehand, not ruled, so no two circles or squares match.

Colored Composition of Forms - August Ma.title: Colored Composition of Forms
facts: This is one of Macke's most abstract works, part of a 'Colored Forms' series painted just months before his death.
Macke was a founding member of Der Blaue Reiter, the Blue Rider circle of German Expressionists.
In April 1914 he traveled to Tunisia with Paul Klee and Louis Moilliet, a trip whose intense light transformed his use of color.
He was killed in action on the Western Front in September 1914, at just 27, only months after making this work.
The painting is held by the Albertina museum in Vienna.

Compenetrazione iridescente n. 4 (Studio.title: Compenetrazione iridescente n. 4 (Studio della luce)
facts: In his Iridescent Interpenetration series, Balla tried to separate the pure experience of light from the objects we usually see it on.
The effects of light and movement are reduced to interlocking triangles in rainbow colours.
The series grew out of his stay in Dusseldorf in the winter of 1912 to 1913, where he was decorating a private house.
These works marked a turning point toward abstraction in Balla's Futurist painting.
He was drawn to scientific ideas about light and colour, which he merged with his interest in theosophy.

Composition - Vicente do Rego Monteiro 1.title: Composition
facts: Rego Monteiro helped introduce European modern art to Brazil, returning from Paris in 1930 with about a hundred School of Paris works to exhibit.
He exhibited at the Salon des Independants in Paris in 1913, when he was only thirteen.
He participated in Sao Paulo's 1922 Modern Art Week, the launch of Brazilian modernism.
His art drew on the geometry of Marajoara ceramics, made by the ancient peoples of Marajo Island in the Amazon delta.
He spent much of his life between France and Brazil and worked as a poet and publisher alongside painting.

Composition 10 in Black and White - Piet.title: Composition 10 in Black and White
facts: Also called Pier and Ocean, the work grew from drawings Mondrian made of breakwaters and waves at the Dutch seaside resorts of Domburg and Scheveningen.
It is the first painting in which Mondrian worked exclusively in black and white, marking a turning point on his path to pure abstraction.
The long horizontal lines stand in for rolling waves while the verticals below suggest a wooden pier reaching into the sea.
The painting is held at the Kroller-Muller Museum in Otterlo in the Netherlands.

Composition A - Piet Mondrian 1920.jpg.title: Composition A
facts: Painted soon after Mondrian helped found the De Stijl movement, the work pares his vocabulary down to black lines, grays, and the three primary colors.
Mondrian called his mature abstract style Neoplasticism, seeking universal harmony through only straight lines and flat planes of color.
The painting is held by the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna in Rome.

Composition no. II - Piet Mondrian 1913..title: Composition no. II
facts: The near-abstract grid grew from landscapes along the River Gein near Amsterdam, with a row of trees, a farm, and their reflection reduced to lines.
Mondrian painted it during his Cubist years in Paris, when he still took dunes, trees, and facades as starting points before leaving nature behind.
The painting is held at the Kroller-Muller Museum in Otterlo in the Netherlands.

Composition V - Wassily Kandinsky 1911.j.title: Composition V
facts: A Munich artists' group rejected it for breaking their size limit, so Kandinsky and Franz Marc walked out and founded the Blue Rider.
It then hung in the very first Blue Rider exhibition, the show that announced the breakaway group.
Kandinsky reserved the word Composition for his most ambitious works, each one built up from many preparatory studies.
He completed only ten Compositions in his life; the first three were later destroyed during the Second World War.
The canvas is large, nearly two meters tall and almost three wide, meant to surround the viewer.
Kandinsky had synesthesia and titled these works like music, treating color and line the way a composer treats sound.

Composition VII - Wassily Kandinsky 1913.title: Composition VII
facts: Kandinsky prepared for months and made around thirty studies, then painted the huge canvas in just a few days in late November 1913.
Beneath the swirling abstraction lie themes of the Apocalypse, the Flood, Resurrection and the Garden of Eden.
It is often called one of the greatest masterpieces of early abstract art.
The painting belongs to the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.
Kandinsky believed colours and forms could affect the soul much as music does, an idea that drove his move into abstraction.

Composition VIII - Wassily Kandinsky 192.title: Composition VIII
facts: Painted soon after Kandinsky joined the Bauhaus, where its clean, rational spirit pushed his work toward crisp geometry.
It marks his break from the swirling, organic abstraction of his Munich years into circles, triangles, and grids.
Kandinsky believed geometric shapes carried feeling, and meant the forms to ring out like notes of music.
He gave the circle special weight, treating it as a calm, complete form among the sharper angles.
It hangs at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York, which holds a deep collection of his work.

Composition with Grid #1 - Piet Mondrian.title: Composition with Grid No. 1
facts: X-ray study revealed that Mondrian first laid down a regular grid of rectangles based on the golden ratio beneath the finished surface.
It is an early work in the style Mondrian developed after co-founding the Dutch group De Stijl in 1917.
The painting is held by the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

Conway Castle, North Wales - J.M.W. Turn.title: Conway Castle, North Wales
facts: Turner toured Wales in his early twenties, sketching medieval castles that became some of his first celebrated watercolors.
This watercolor depicts Conwy Castle, a 13th-century fortress built for King Edward I on the north coast of Wales.
Turner worked the sheet in watercolor and gum arabic over a graphite drawing; it is now in the J. Paul Getty Museum.

Corpus Christi Procession - Amadeo de So.title: Corpus Christi Procession (Procissao Corpus Christi)
facts: The scene comes from the Catholic religious processions the artist watched near his family home in rural northern Portugal.
He painted it in oil on a small wood panel, only about 29 by 51 centimeters across.
The picture entered the Gulbenkian collection in Lisbon as a gift from the artist's widow, Lucie de Souza Cardoso.
Souza Cardoso folded the village ritual into a cubist framework, bridging Portuguese tradition and the new art he met in Paris.

Cosmic Energy 4 (Energía cosmica 4) - Le.title: Cosmic Energy 4 (Energía cosmica 4)
facts: Nierman trained as a violinist before turning to painting, and said music's movement and harmony shaped everything he made.
He first studied business and worked in accounting, taking up art seriously only after deciding he was not gifted enough for a music career.
His swirling abstractions evoke cosmic and natural forces, and admirers nicknamed him Mexico's answer to Jackson Pollock.
He cited composers Bach and Debussy alongside painters Kandinsky and Miro as influences on his work.
Born in Mexico City in 1932 to Lithuanian and Ukrainian parents, he became one of Mexico's most internationally exhibited artists.

Cycle 1961 - S.2 - Emilio Vedova 1961.jp.title: Cycle 1961 - S.2
facts: Vedova worked sheets of newspaper into the paint, letting headlines surface through it because he saw news and history as the raw material of his art.
Bursts of colour and slashing lines stand against a black ground, staging what he called a 'clash of situations.'
A self-taught painter from Venice, Vedova joined the anti-Fascist Resistance during the Second World War.
He won the Grand Prize for Painting at the 1960 Venice Biennale, the year before this work.

Daddy Longlegs of the Evening - Hope! -.title: Daddy Longlegs of the Evening - Hope!
facts: This was the first painting Dalí finished after fleeing wartime Europe for the United States, made in Bowling Green, Virginia.
The title comes from an old French saying, 'Araignée du soir, espoir,' meaning a spider seen at evening is a sign of hope.
It became the first Dalí painting bought by collectors Reynolds and Eleanor Morse, who went on to amass the collection now in St. Petersburg, Florida.
The winged, draped figure rising at the right echoes the ancient Greek statue known as the Winged Victory of Samothrace.
The melting central head is another of Dalí's soft self-portraits, surrounded by symbols of a world at war.

Vrubel paints the demon as a brooding, longing figure searching for harmony rather than a creature of pure evil.
His faceted, crystal-edged brushwork, applied with a palette knife, makes the surface read almost like stained glass.
It was Vrubel's first large canvas, painted soon after he moved to Moscow in 1889, and was harshly received at first.

facts: This is a sculpture, not a painting, assembling a galloping horse and the houses behind it into one fused form.
Boccioni made it from a mix of unlikely materials, including gouache, oil, wood, cardboard, copper, and coated iron.
It puts into practice his manifesto on Futurist sculpture, which urged artists to combine many materials and reject closed, solid forms.
Few of his sculptures survive, which makes this assemblage especially rare.
The work belongs to the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice.

Dipinto - Sam Francis 1957.jpg.title: Dipinto
facts: Francis began painting while recovering from a plane crash in a body cast, working on canvases propped above his hospital bed.
An Air Force flying accident in World War II left him with spinal tuberculosis and years in hospital, where art took hold.
He lived in Paris from 1950 to 1957, drawn to the loose, gestural Tachisme then sweeping French painting.
Francis often left large stretches of canvas bare, letting bright pools and drips of color float against white space.

Disc-Relief (Relief-Disques) - Robert De.title: Disc-Relief (Relief-Disques)
facts: Built from rings of pure color, it was made with gouache and sand worked over pencil, so the surface has a faint grit you can almost feel.
Late in life Delaunay circled back to the spinning disc, a shape he had chased for over twenty years as the simplest way to set color in motion.
He believed color alone, with no objects, could carry a painting; the eye supplies the movement as warm and cool circles push against each other.

Doubled Back - Bev Doolittle 1988.jpg.title: Doubled Back
facts: Doolittle hides a grizzly bear in plain sight: the animal has doubled back along its own trail and crouches in the brush at the very front of the scene, watching you.
Fresh bear tracks lead up the snowy path, setting up the work's quiet question of how close the grizzly really is.
The painting belongs to Doolittle's signature 'camouflage' style, where the background resolves into a hidden animal once your eye adjusts.
Like most of her work, it was painted in watercolor, a medium she brought into a Western-art genre long dominated by oils.
It was published as a limited-edition print by The Greenwich Workshop, the Connecticut firm that issued nearly all of Doolittle's editions.

Dusty Road II - Mihály Munkácsy 1884.jpg.title: Dusty Road II
facts: Hungary's most famous painter of the era, Munkácsy was such a celebrity in Paris that crowds queued around the block for single-painting shows.
The picture captures sunlight breaking through the cloud of dust kicked up by a passing peasant cart.
He painted it after spending time in Barbizon, where he turned from dark genre scenes toward fresher, more colorful landscapes.
It is painted in oil on wood and hangs in the Hungarian National Gallery in Budapest.

El Castillo - Leonardo Nierman 1932-2023.title: El Castillo
facts: Nierman studied the violin from childhood, and the rhythm and movement of music remained the core of his abstract painting.
He earned a business degree and worked in accounting before committing fully to art.
His vivid, flame-like canvases suggest fire, water, birds, and celestial events rendered as pure color and motion.
Critics dubbed him Mexico's Jackson Pollock for his energetic abstraction.
He was a prolific sculptor and muralist as well as a painter, exhibiting worldwide across a long career.

Elasticità - Umberto Boccioni 1912.jpg.title: Elasticita (Elasticity)
facts: The painting compresses a galloping horse and its rider into a single charged blur of motion against a city backdrop.
The title points to the Futurist fascination with the stretch and spring of muscle and matter in movement.
Boccioni painted it the same year he visited Paris and absorbed the lessons of the Cubist sculptors there.
The canvas is almost exactly square, about a meter on each side.

En tono mayor - Carlos Mérida 1981.jpg.title: En tono mayor
facts: Mérida fused Maya symbols and Guatemalan folk motifs with European Cubism and geometric abstraction.
Guatemalan-born, he became a naturalized Mexican and worked alongside the muralists while pursuing pure abstraction.
He made this late in life, near age 90, in his mature style of crisp interlocking geometric figures.
The title means 'In a major key,' borrowing a musical term for the bright, ordered rhythm of its shapes.

Endormies - Rupert Bunny c. 1904.jpg.title: Endormies
facts: The sleeping figure was modelled on the painter's wife, Jeanne Morel, who posed for many of his languid Belle Epoque compositions.
Bunny was the first Australian to win an award at the Paris Salon, taking a prize in 1890.
The National Gallery of Victoria bought the picture in 1911 for 500 guineas through its Felton Bequest.
By the end of his career the French state had acquired 13 of Bunny's works, more than from any other Australian artist.
The painting was shown at London's Royal Academy in 1904, part of the artist's run of European exhibitions.

Luce was one of the founders of Neo-Impressionism alongside Seurat and Signac, applying scientific color theory to landscape in tiny separate touches of paint.
Camille Pissarro introduced Luce to the Neo-Impressionist circle in 1887, and he quickly became a committed convert to the new method.

facts: Hamilton was nicknamed 'the American Turner' for the glowing, atmospheric light of his seascapes.
He sailed to England in 1854 specifically to study the work of J. M. W. Turner and other British landscape painters.
Born in Ireland, Hamilton emigrated to Philadelphia as a boy and worked as a drawing teacher and illustrator before painting full time.
The canvas is inscribed on the back 'Evening on the Seashore / Jas Hamilton / Philad 1864', tying it to his home city's harbor.

Evening on the Seine - Birge Harrison c..title: Evening on the Seine
facts: Harrison was a leading American Tonalist, favoring quiet, subdued color over the bright palette of the Impressionists.
He drew on the romantic, moody nature of the Barbizon school rather than the high-keyed effects of his French contemporaries.
Known for winter scenes, he sought the soft effects of dusk, fog and snow on the landscape.
His brother Alexander Harrison was also a noted American painter who worked in France.
The painting belongs to the North Carolina Museum of Art in Raleigh.

It was the largest painting he had made up to that point, roughly six and a half feet tall and eight feet wide.
He said his starting point was an image of women working in a rice field from the 1949 Italian film Bitter Rice.
Hidden in the tangle of hooked lines are bits of bodies and animals: eyes, teeth, jaws, and shapes of birds and fish.

facts: Prendergast returned again and again to crowds of elegantly dressed women and children at the seaside.
His scenes are built from a patchwork of bright color dabs often likened to mosaic.
Unlike his fellow members of The Eight, he avoided gritty city subjects in favor of parks, beaches, and promenades.
He worked in oil, watercolor, and monotype, a printmaking method that yields a single unique impression.
His close brother Charles was a noted craftsman who made hand-carved frames, several of them for Maurice's paintings.

Flower by the Shore - August Strindberg.title: Flower by the Shore
facts: August Strindberg is far better known as a Swedish playwright and novelist; painting was one of several pursuits alongside photography and amateur science.
He painted intuitively in short, intense bursts, working the paint with a palette knife rather than carefully rendering what he saw.
Most of the roughly 117 paintings accepted as his were made within just a few years.
This work is held by the Malmo Art Museum in Sweden.

Forest - Kazuo Nakamura 1953.jpg.title: Forest
facts: The broken, dabbed brushwork echoes Cezanne, whose paintings Nakamura had just seen reproduced in a 1952 issue of Life magazine.
It was one of four works shown at the first Painters Eleven exhibition that entered the Robert McLaughlin Gallery's permanent collection.
As a teenager Nakamura was among the 22,000 Japanese Canadians interned during the Second World War, at the Tashme camp in British Columbia.
His restrained, near-monochrome style set him apart from the bolder abstraction of his Painters Eleven colleagues.
He said he was always drawn to 'the law of order that lies in everything,' seeking the structures shared by nature, science, and math.

Four Sunflowers Gone to Seed - Vincent v.title: Four Sunflowers Gone to Seed
facts: Painted in Paris two years before the famous vase sunflowers - here the flowers lie cut and drying, almost life-size.
Paul Gauguin admired the Paris sunflower studies and traded his own work to own two of them.
It belongs to the Kröller-Müller Museum in the Netherlands, home to one of the largest van Gogh collections in the world.
These cut-stem studies let him explore the oranges and yellows he would later make famous in the Arles bouquets.

facts: Lee founded Mono-ha, Japan's first internationally recognized contemporary art movement, focused on raw materials and space.
Each line was drawn top to bottom in one breath, the loaded brush fading as it ran, like a controlled exhale.
The repetition grew out of calligraphy he practiced as a child in Korea, demanding command of mind, body, and brush.
The work pushes back against the ego of Abstract Expressionism, showing painting instead as a calm, timed process.

Frost at Giverny - Claude Monet 1885.jpg.title: Frost at Giverny
facts: Monet painted outdoors in all weather, once with a hot water bottle and three coats, chasing the pink light that frost gives a field at dawn.
He had settled in Giverny in 1883, renting the house and grounds he would later buy and transform into his famous garden.
Monet returned to frozen and snow-covered fields again and again, fascinated by how white surfaces catch tints of blue, rose, and gold.

Futurist Composition - Joseph Stella 191.title: Futurist Composition
facts: Stella worked this composition in pastel over graphite, translating the dazzle of electric light into shards of pure color.
It grows out of his fascination with Coney Island, whose nighttime glare he turned into one of America's earliest abstract works.
Born in a mountain village in southern Italy, Stella met the Futurists on visits to Paris and Italy before bringing their charge to New York.
He first came to America in 1896 to study medicine, then switched to art at the Art Students League the next year.

Gardiner's Bay from Sag Harbor - George.title: Gardiner's Bay from Sag Harbor
facts: A teenage work - Bellows was about 17 - painted years before the gritty New York boxing scenes that made him famous.
It is an early watercolor on paper from his high school days, not the bold oils he later became known for.
Bellows' mother was the daughter of a Sag Harbor whaling captain, and the family summered at this quiet eastern end of Long Island.
The work belongs to the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

Gávea Golf - Lucílio de Albuquerque c. 1.title: Gávea Golf
facts: Gavea is a district of Rio de Janeiro beneath a steep granite peak, where Brazil's first golf course opened in the 1920s.
Albuquerque was a Rio painter and teacher known for landscapes and portraits; after his death his wife Georgina turned their home into a museum of his work.
His wife, Georgina de Albuquerque, was herself a noted painter, and the two were among the leading Brazilian artists of their generation.

Giant Magnolias on a Blue Velvet Cloth -.title: Giant Magnolias on a Blue Velvet Cloth
facts: Widely judged one of the finest still lifes of Heade's whole career, with bright blooms glowing against a dark ground.
He painted it after settling in Saint Augustine, Florida, where the railroad magnate Henry Flagler became his only major patron.
Heade laid flowers flat on velvet cloth rather than arranging them in vases, an unusual choice for the period.
The magnolia and rose pieces cap a career otherwise known for seascapes and shimmering hummingbird-and-orchid scenes.
The National Gallery of Art in Washington acquired the painting in 1982.

Grainstacks at Giverny, the Evening Sun.title: Grainstacks at Giverny, the Evening Sun
facts: An early entry in the grainstack obsession that became Monet's famous series - he eventually painted the stacks more than 25 times.
The stacks stood just outside his door at Giverny; he had canvases carried out in a wheelbarrow to catch each light.
These were no small heaps: the stacks of harvested grain stood taller than a person, built to shed rain until threshing.
Monet chose the late hour deliberately, when low sun turns the stacks to glowing forms against a cooling sky.

Grande composizione A con nero rosso gri.title: Grande composizione A con nero rosso grigio giallo e blu (Great Composition A with Black, Red, Gray, Yellow and Blue)
facts: This is among the first fully Neo-Plastic works Mondrian made after settling in Paris, marking his break from Cubism into pure abstraction.
It restricts itself to primary colours with black, grey and white, the disciplined vocabulary Mondrian would refine for the rest of his life.
Mondrian helped found De Stijl, the Dutch movement whose name means The Style.
The painting is held by the National Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art in Rome.

Haystacks, End of Summer - Claude Monet.title: Haystacks, End of Summer
facts: From the series that made Monet rich: fifteen were shown together in 1891 and sold out within days.
Kandinsky later said seeing one of these haystacks was the moment he realized painting didn't need a subject.
Monet worked several canvases at once, switching as the light moved, sometimes finishing only a few minutes of work on each before the moment passed.
Showing the same stacks across seasons and hours was a radical idea: the true subject was changing light, not the stacks themselves.

Head (Self-portrait as P. Kubínčan) - Ar.title: Head (Self-portrait as P. Kubínčan)
facts: A Slovak Expressionist known for intense, brooding portraits; much of his surviving work entered Slovak national collections after his death in 1944.
Born Arnold Weisz to a Jewish family, he added 'Kubínčan' after Dolný Kubín, the Slovak town where he grew up.
He absorbed Expressionism while studying at the Academy of Fine Arts in Berlin around 1918.
Before deportation he packed nearly 300 of his works into a single suitcase, which a friend carried to America and returned to Slovakia decades later.
Horses in motion recur throughout his paintings and drawings as a favorite motif.

Helene's Florist - Richard Estes 1971.jp.title: Helene's Florist
facts: Estes painted New York storefronts from his own photographs, sharpening reflections until the painting outdoes the photo.
Look closely: every pane of glass carries its own reflected street scene, painted by hand.
The shop stood at Columbus Avenue and 72nd Street in Manhattan, the source for this picture.
Estes combined sharp focus at every distance, something a single camera lens cannot capture in one frame.
His city scenes are almost always empty of people, turning busy streets into still, glassy stages.

Hide and Seek - Bev Doolittle 1990.jpg.title: Hide and Seek
facts: Doolittle set herself the task of hiding pinto ponies among rocks and snow, blending each horse so completely into its wintry surroundings that it nearly vanishes.
The full work is built from twenty-four separate images; only when all are seen together do the letters spelling 'Hide and Seek' emerge from the rocks and horses.
The project took over a year to complete and was released as a boxed portfolio of six prints in a gold-stamped linen case.
Pinto ponies and the American West were lifelong subjects for Doolittle, who roamed the Southwest in a motorhome painting on location early in her career.
It was issued in a 1990 limited edition of 25,000 by The Greenwich Workshop.

Icarus - Lee Krasner 1964.jpg.title: Icarus
facts: Krasner painted her boldest large canvases at night during bouts of insomnia after Jackson Pollock's death, working in his old barn studio.
The title nods to the Greek youth Icarus, who flew too near the sun on wax wings and fell to his death.
It belongs to a run of vivid, large color works Krasner made in the mid-1960s, alongside paintings like 'Siren.'
She had spent the prior years on the somber brown 'Umber' or 'Night Journeys' paintings before returning to strong color here.

Il bevitore - Umberto Boccioni 1914.jpg.title: Il bevitore (The Drinker)
facts: The subject is a man muddled by drink, slumped over a table and seen from a steep angle above.
Boccioni broke the figure and the room into faceted planes, showing how closely he had studied Cubism.
He painted it in 1914, the same year he published his book on Futurist painting and sculpture.

Il romanzo di una cucitrice - Umberto Bo.title: Il romanzo di una cucitrice (The Novel of a Seamstress)
facts: An early work, painted two years before Boccioni signed the manifesto that launched Futurist painting in 1910.
It shows a young woman absorbed in a book, with her sewing machine set beside her.
The pairing sets manual labor against the life of the mind, a deliberate contrast at the heart of the picture.
Shown in Milan in 1908, it met with little praise and many harsh reviews at the time.
The large canvas, about 150 by 170 centimeters, is held in the Barilla collection of modern art in Parma.

Improvisation 26 (Rowing) - Wassily Kand.title: Improvisation 26 (Rowing)
facts: Look for the rowers in the dark diagonal lines, the slanted strokes standing in for oars dipping into water.
Kandinsky used Improvisation for works that came spontaneously from inside him, without planning.
The single word Rowing in the title is just a hint, leaving you to find the scene inside the color.
It is held at the Lenbachhaus in Munich, a major home for Blue Rider painting.
He made it as he stood on the edge of pure abstraction, the boat almost dissolving into pattern.

Improvisation Sintflut (Deluge) - Wassil.title: Improvisation Sintflut (Deluge)
facts: Sintflut is German for the great flood, the deluge from the Bible's story of the world washed clean.
Kandinsky returned again and again to such end-of-the-world scenes, painting a storm before a fresh start.
A surge of restless color reads as a rolling wave, with a shaft of light breaking through the center.
It belongs to the Lenbachhaus in Munich, holder of one of the great Blue Rider collections.
Improvisation was his name for paintings that poured out unplanned, straight from feeling.

In the Dunes (In de Duinen) - Vincent va.title: In the Dunes (In de Duinen)
facts: Painted during van Gogh's early Dutch years near The Hague, when his palette was still dark and earth-toned, years before the vivid color of his French work.
He was largely self-taught at this stage, having decided to become an artist only a few years earlier at about age twenty-seven.
The Hague dunes and beach gave him cheap, open subjects close to home while he taught himself to paint outdoors.

Iris, Tulips, Jonquils, and Crocuses - A.title: Iris, Tulips, Jonquils, and Crocuses
facts: The painting hangs in the National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington, the city where Thomas lived and worked for most of her life.
Despite their spontaneous look, works like this were planned, often from watercolor studies and free-hand pencil marks drawn on the canvas first.
Thomas drew her color and movement directly from nature, studying the flowers and trees in her yard and in Washington parks.
The vertical bands of color are built from many small tile-like strokes, a style sometimes called her Alma stripes.
She painted it in 1969, the year she retired fully into painting in her late seventies and her reputation began to rise.

Irises - Vincent van Gogh 1890.jpg.title: Irises
facts: Painted in the asylum garden at Saint-Rémy, where van Gogh called painting 'the lightning conductor for my illness'.
He thought of the irises as studies, but they now rank among his most loved works.
He made these flower still lifes in a burst of work during his final weeks at the asylum, before leaving for Auvers in May 1890.
The blooms were once more pink and purple, but a red pigment he used has faded over time, cooling the colors.

Irises - Vincent van GoghMay 1890.jpg.title: Irises
facts: Painted in his final weeks at the Saint-Remy asylum, one of just four ambitious flower still lifes he made there before leaving in May 1890.
Van Gogh set the violet blooms against a pink ground for a soft, harmonious effect, but the red pigment has faded so the background now reads bluish.
He worked at the bouquets quickly and intensely, calling such painting a way to stay calm in the weeks before he checked himself out of the asylum.

facts: Von Guerard sketched the mountains of the Red Sea coast from a steamship during his 1882 voyage home from Australia to Europe.
He worked the studio oil up from drawings made on deck, not on the spot.
Austrian-born, he spent decades in Australia and became the first master of the National Gallery of Victoria's art school.
The small panel is painted in oil on cardboard and signed 'Eugen von Guérard'.
It belongs to the Art Gallery of New South Wales, a 1970 gift from Frank McDonald.

It is watercolor over graphite on paper, the medium Homer prized for catching tropical light quickly and directly.
The crew hauls the anchor to set sail, with a faint line of palm-fringed land marking the Key West shore behind them.

facts: Renoir and Monet set up their easels side by side at this riverside bathing spot in 1869, racing to capture the same scene of summer leisure.
La Grenouillere, 'the frog pond,' was a floating cafe and bathing resort on the Seine near Bougival, reachable by train from Paris.
These quick, dappled studies of light on water are often cited as among the first true Impressionist paintings, made years before the movement had a name.
Renoir kept his palette light, mostly blues and greens, with soft feathery strokes that let the trees melt into the water below.

La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse - C.title: La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse

La Tour - Robert Delaunay 1926.jpg.title: La Tour (The Eiffel Tower)
facts: Delaunay painted the Eiffel Tower obsessively, first in a major series around 1909 to 1912, then returning to the subject in a fresh way through the 1920s.
For his tower paintings he worked partly from aerial photographs taken in 1909 from the basket of a hot-air balloon high above Paris.
He saw the tower both as a symbol of French progress and as the ideal scaffold for building a bold new language of pure abstraction.

Lake Brienz, with the Setting Moon - J..title: Lake Brienz, with the Setting Moon
facts: Turner made glowing watercolors of the Swiss lakes on his late Alpine tours in the early 1840s, dissolving mountains and water into pure light.
Lake Brienz lies in the Bernese Oberland of Switzerland, fed by Alpine glaciers that give its water a vivid turquoise color.
Turner first toured the Alps in 1802 and returned repeatedly in his final decade, sketching the Swiss lakes from memory back in his London studio.

Landscape - Kazuo Nakamura 1952.jpg.title: Landscape
facts: Nakamura was a founding member of Painters Eleven, the Toronto group that helped bring abstraction to wider Canadian audiences.
As a teenager he was among the 22,000 Japanese Canadians interned during the Second World War, at the Tashme camp near Hope, British Columbia.
Barred from returning to British Columbia after the war, he settled in Toronto, where his career began in the early 1950s.

Landscape by Chinese Ink - Takeuchi Seih.title: Landscape by Chinese Ink
facts: Takeuchi Seiho was a leading painter of the Kyoto art world and a central figure in modern nihonga, Japanese-style painting.
He blended the realism of the traditional Maruyama-Shijo school with techniques he admired in Western painters like Turner and Corot.
He is especially celebrated for his monochrome ink landscapes, which carry that fusion of Japanese tradition and Western realism.

Landscape from Saint-Rémy - Vincent van.title: Landscape from Saint-Rémy
facts: Van Gogh painted this view from the window of his room at the Saint-Paul asylum, returning to the same scene to catch changing weather and seasons.
Rolling, serpentine brushstrokes give the fields and clouds a restless, swirling motion typical of his late work.

Though signed 1881, the picture was likely painted earlier, during the unusually harsh winter of 1879 to 1880.

Courbet was so attached to the picture that he kept it for himself and carried it with him when he fled into exile in Switzerland in 1873.

He aimed to capture the simultaneous events, views and sensations of the modern metropolis, all glimpsed at once through a single frame.

Paris Street - Robert Delaunay 1906.jpg.title: Paris Street
facts: Around 1906 Delaunay worked in a Neo-Impressionist vein, building forms from small squares of color that read like a mosaic.
He often left patches of bare canvas showing through to suggest space and light, his love of brilliant color already plain at this early stage.
Rather than copy Seurat's tiny dots, he experimented with the interaction of larger contrasting color areas, a path that led him toward abstraction.

facts: The boulevards look new because they were: Haussmann had just rebuilt Paris, and Caillebotte painted the city still feeling unfamiliar to its own residents.

The canvas is enormous, over six feet tall and nine feet wide, so the strolling couple meet you nearly life-sized at the edge of the frame.
A central green lamppost splits the picture in two, a deliberate use of two-point perspective to pull the eye down the rain-slicked cobbles.
Caillebotte was fascinated by photography, and the way a figure is sharply cropped at the right edge echoes a snapshot caught mid-stride.

facts: Painted in poet Celia Thaxter's island garden off the New Hampshire coast, a summer colony for artists and writers.
Hassam set up his easel on the shaded porch of Thaxter's cottage, looking out over her famous flower garden toward an outcrop called Babb's Rock.
The Isles of Shoals are nine small, rocky, treeless islands; the painting was made on Appledore, the largest of them.
The view was a Hassam favorite, and he painted this stretch of poppies and sea many times across his summers there.

She collected sun-bleached animal bones from the desert and shipped barrels of them back east, finding them beautiful rather than morbid.
Pairing a dry skull with a living flower sets death and life side by side in one calm image, a contrast she returned to often.

facts: Hidden eagles are camouflaged among the birch trees; look closely and you can pick out their distinctive beaks emerging from the bark.
The scene shows a trapper and his horses spooked into flight after stumbling onto ground held sacred, the eagles standing in for watching ancestral spirits.
The work draws on the reverence that peoples such as the Blackfeet, Sioux, and Crow held for lands considered holy.
It is a classic example of Doolittle's camouflage technique, in which details can be read in more than one way depending on how you look.
Doolittle painted it in watercolor and it was published as a limited-edition print by The Greenwich Workshop.

Saint-Tropez - Maximilien Luce 1897.jpg.title: Saint-Tropez
facts: Luce first visited Saint-Tropez in 1892 alongside Paul Signac, who soon bought a house in the old port and settled there.
By this date Luce was replacing the tiny dots of strict pointillism with longer dashes of color, set so neighboring hues glow against each other.
Saint-Tropez was then a quiet Mediterranean fishing town, decades before its fame as a glamorous resort.
The Neo-Impressionists prized the brilliant southern light of the Riviera for testing their theories of divided color.

San Fransisco - Brooke Borcherding 2023..title: San Fransisco
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 24 by 36 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk - Claude Mo.title: San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk
facts: Monet painted the church of San Giorgio Maggiore across the water as the setting sun lit its tower; he made several versions at different times of day.
This came from Monet's only trip to Venice, in the autumn of 1908, when he was sixty-eight and traveling with his wife Alice.
He began the views on the spot but finished them from memory back in his studio at Giverny in France, calling Venice almost too beautiful to paint.
Welsh collector Gwendoline Davies bought this canvas and later left it to the National Museum in Cardiff, where it hangs today.
Monet held the Venice paintings back for years, finally showing twenty-nine of them in Paris in 1912 to wide acclaim.

Scene Under the Arcades in Thun - August.title: Scene Under the Arcades in Thun
facts: Thun is a Swiss town on Lake Thun whose old town is lined with covered arcades, called Lauben in German.
Macke lived near Lake Thun from autumn 1913 to spring 1914, an intensely productive eight months.
He was a founding member of Der Blaue Reiter, the Blue Rider Expressionist group.
The strolling shoppers and townsfolk under the arcades typify his lifelong interest in everyday public life.
The work is held by the Museum Kunstpalast in Dusseldorf.

Seascape near Les Saintes-Maries-de-la-M.title: Seascape near Les Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer
facts: Van Gogh painted this on the beach during a week's trip from Arles to a small Mediterranean fishing village, his first real look at the sea in the south.
He worked so close to the surf that grains of beach sand are still embedded in the dried paint.
He wrote that the sea's color kept changing 'like a mackerel,' shifting between green, purple, blue, pink and grey from one moment to the next.
The painting now hangs in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

Season of the Eagle - Bev Doolittle 1987.title: Season of the Eagle
facts: An eagle is hidden in the snow of the mountain pass, a shape Doolittle said she was especially glad to find given the bird's sacred place in Native American belief.
A line of Native American riders crosses a snowy pass at the foot of a mountain, their reflection mirrored in a still, glassy lake.
The work reflects the belief Doolittle described, that all creatures share one creator and are therefore brothers.
It belongs to her camouflage style, where the landscape itself resolves into a hidden image once the eye finds it.
It was published in 1987 in a limited edition of 36,548 prints by The Greenwich Workshop.

Seattle Haze - Brooke Borcherding August.title: Seattle Haze

Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Seattle Skyline - Brooke Borcherding Dec.title: Seattle Skyline

facts: Acrylic on canvas, 36 by 48 inches.
