Self-Portrait - Vincent van Gogh 1887.jp.title: Self-Portrait
facts: During his two years in Paris, van Gogh painted at least two dozen self-portraits, often because he could not afford to pay models.
The flickering dots and dashes of color show him testing the Neo-Impressionist pointillist technique he met in Paris.
He set blue-green tones in the background to make the orange-red of his hair and beard glow by contrast.
This small study was painted on artist's board rather than canvas and now hangs at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Self-Portrait - Vincent van Gogh 1889.jp.title: Self-Portrait
facts: Painted at the Saint-Rémy asylum after a mental health crisis, when van Gogh said he wanted to show he had grown calmer.
The rippling blue background echoes the swirling sky of The Starry Night from the same period.
It is likely one of the last self-portraits he ever made, created not long before he left the asylum.
He painted himself in three-quarter view holding his palette, presenting himself plainly as a working artist.

Series I White & Blue Flower Shapes - Ge.title: Series I White & Blue Flower Shapes
facts: A single petal-like form swells against a warm red ground, blurring the line between an abstract shape and a blossom.
It comes from an early series in which O'Keeffe worked out the close-up flower compositions she became famous for a decade later.
The painting is oil on board, a firmer surface than canvas that suited her smooth, blended transitions of color.
It is held by the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe.

Series I, No. 10 - Georgia O'Keeffe 1919.title: Series I, No. 10
facts: Pale curving shapes can be read as a flower or as a lake, treetops, and a dark mountain, holding still life and landscape in one image.
O'Keeffe painted it at Lake George in the Adirondacks, where her future husband's family kept a summer home she often worked at.
The piece shows how she fused abstraction with the natural world rather than choosing between them.
It belongs to the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe.

Shrovetide - Boris Kustodiev 1916.jpg.title: Shrovetide (Maslenitsa)
facts: Maslenitsa is the Russian folk festival of the last week before Lent, when families feast on hot blini before the long fast begins.
Kustodiev painted this entirely from memory of provincial Russia, working from a wheelchair after spinal tuberculosis paralyzed his legs.
He returned to the Maslenitsa theme repeatedly, painting separate versions in 1916, 1919 and 1920.
The glowing pink-and-gold sky over the snowbound town shows his love of an idealized, festive old Russia rather than any single real place.

Simultaneous Windows (2nd Motif, 1st Par.title: Simultaneous Windows (1st Part, 2nd Motif) (Les Fenêtres simultanées sur la ville)
facts: The green wedge near the center is the Eiffel Tower, dissolved into panes of color until the city becomes pure light.
It belongs to a burst of about twenty 'Windows' canvases Delaunay painted in a single year, 1912, as he crossed over into near-abstract painting.
He chased what he called simultaneity: placing colors side by side so they react in the eye, an idea he took from the color scientist Chevreul.
Delaunay and his wife Sonia worked out these color ideas together, treating the window not as a view but as a screen of overlapping light.

SLU - Brooke Borcherding June 2018.jpg.title: SLU
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 24 by 30 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Snow White without the Dwarves - Ghada A.title: Snow White without the Dwarves
facts: Amer builds her images by stitching threads onto the canvas, then letting loose ends hang and tangle, so the work reads as both embroidery and painting.
Born in Cairo in 1963 and raised in France, she has long used a craft historically tied to women's domestic work to make pointed statements about female identity.
The piece belongs to the Barjeel Art Foundation, a Sharjah collection devoted to modern and contemporary Arab art.

Snow, Boulevard de Clichy, Paris - Paul.title: Snow, Boulevard de Clichy, Paris
facts: Painted the year Signac and Seurat unveiled Pointillism at the final Impressionist exhibition - this snowy street is one of its first tests.
Signac met Seurat in 1884 and, struck by his color theories, traded Impressionism's loose strokes for tiny dots of pure pigment.
He was self-taught, turning to painting at eighteen after Monet's first solo show convinced him to give up plans to be an architect.

Sonata de la piedra y de la carne - Mari.title: Sonata de la piedra y de la carne
facts: Carreño was a Cuban-Chilean painter whose style merged Cubist abstraction, Surrealism, and the look of Mexican mural painting.
The work belongs to his 'Un mundo petrificado' (A Petrified World) series, where bodies seem to harden into stone.
After a decade working in geometric abstraction, Carreño returned to figurative painting in the 1960s, partly in response to what he had seen of postwar Europe.

South Whidbey Shores - Brooke Borcherdin.title: South Whidbey Shores
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 15 by 30 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Spectra Four Seasons - Douglas Coupland.title: Spectra Four Seasons
facts: Coupland built this work from rows of coloured pencil crayons sealed in Plexiglas, using the spectrum of leads to stand in for the natural world.
It is a set of four pieces, one for each season, each panel about 1.8 metres wide.
Coupland is also a bestselling novelist, best known for 'Generation X,' the 1991 book that popularized the term.
The piece featured in his 2014 Vancouver Art Gallery survey, 'everywhere is anywhere is anything is everything.'

Spring Blossoms - Brooke Borcherding Apr.title: Spring Blossoms
facts: Oil on canvas, 24 by 36 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Square Berlioz (La Place Vintimille) - É.title: Square Berlioz (La Place Vintimille)
facts: Vuillard painted the small Paris square below his apartment window for decades, like a private weather diary.
This view was painted during wartime Paris, the square's calm a quiet act of normalcy.
Vuillard moved to a fifth-floor apartment overlooking the square in 1908 and stayed there for roughly eighteen years.
It is painted in peinture à la colle, a matte glue-based distemper Vuillard favored over oil for its chalky, fresco-like surface.
The square is named for the Romantic composer Hector Berlioz, whose statue once stood at its center.

St. Malo - Maurice Prendergast c. 1907.j.title: St. Malo
facts: Saint-Malo is a walled port city on the coast of Brittany in northwestern France.
Prendergast made a series of works during a 1907 trip to St. Malo and chose several for the landmark 1908 exhibition of The Eight.
That 1907 visit, in which he absorbed Cezanne and the Fauves, pushed him to paint more boldly in oil.
He composed in small dabs of bright color, a patchwork look often called mosaic-like.
Friendships with Edouard Vuillard and Pierre Bonnard in Paris had earlier placed him firmly among the Post-Impressionists.

Starry Night - Vincent van Gogh 1888.jpg.title: Starry Night Over the Rhône
facts: Painted on the bank of the Rhône a short walk from the Yellow House van Gogh rented in Arles.
It captures gas lamps reflecting on the water alongside the stars, blending man-made and natural light.
He painted it about a year before his more famous swirling Starry Night, which he made from memory at Saint-Rémy.
A couple strolls along the riverbank in the foreground, a quiet human note under the night sky.
He picked out the Great Bear constellation overhead, describing it to his brother as sparkling green and pink.

Starry Night and the Astronauts - Alma T.title: Starry Night and the Astronauts
facts: Thomas made this as part of a series sparked by the Apollo moon missions; she was fascinated by space flight and imagined the sky as if seen from above.
She built the picture from short, mosaic-like dabs of color laid in rows, a signature style she developed in her seventies.
She did not paint full time until 1960, at age sixty-nine, after thirty-five years teaching art in Washington, D.C. public schools.
In 1972, the year she made this, she became the first African American woman to have a solo exhibition at the Whitney Museum in New York.
She was the first graduate of Howard University's fine arts program, finishing in 1924.
Though she never flew in a plane, she said she painted as if airborne, watching light and color shift across the world below.

States of Mind - Those Who Go - Umberto.title: States of Mind II: Those Who Go
facts: Part of a triptych about a railway station farewell - this panel is the rush of passengers leaving, splintered by speed and slanting lines.
The Futurists wanted to paint motion and noise itself; Boccioni reworked the whole series after seeing Cubism in Paris.
Boccioni first painted the trilogy in 1911, then redid it late that year after his November trip to Paris sharpened its Cubist edge.
An earlier set of the three subjects exists as charcoal drawings in a softer, Symbolist manner, also now at MoMA.
The three paintings entered the Museum of Modern Art in New York after passing through the collection of Nelson Rockefeller.

Stati d'animo - Gli addii - Umberto Bocc.title: States of Mind I: The Farewells (Stati d'animo: Gli addii)
facts: This is the central panel of a three-part series staged in a railway station, picturing the embraces of a farewell.
It tries to render the emotion and confusion of parting rather than a clear snapshot of the scene.
Boccioni reworked the painting after his late-1911 trip to Paris, bringing a stronger Cubist structure to it.
The triptych is held together in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Stati d'animo - Quelli che restano - Umb.title: States of Mind III: Those Who Stay (Stati d'animo: Quelli che restano)
facts: This panel shows the people left behind on the platform, drawn downward by long vertical lines that suggest gloom and stillness.
It completes a trilogy about a station farewell, opposite the bustle of the travelers who depart.
Boccioni revised the picture after seeing Cubist work in Paris in late 1911.
The three paintings are kept together at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Steamboats, Rotterdam - Paul Signac 1906.title: Steamboats, Rotterdam
facts: Signac loved working harbors - he sailed to dozens of European ports and painted the smoke, cranes, and steam in confetti-like dabs.
He came to Rotterdam in 1906 on his second trip to the Netherlands and was awed by the vitality of its working port.
On a harbor postcard home he wrote: 'From my window! What industriousness! I am enthusiastic, but amazed.'
Smoke and steam let Signac do what he loved most: dissolve solid forms into shimmering veils of separate colored touches.

Storm in the Skerries (The Flying Dutchm.title: Storm in the Skerries (The Flying Dutchman)
facts: Strindberg found the scene at Dalaro in the Stockholm skerries during the summer of 1892.
He named it for Wagner's opera, casting the storm-tossed sea as the doomed, ever-wandering captain of The Flying Dutchman.
It is one of his largest paintings, and the violence of the sea is built up with fierce, thick strokes of the palette knife.
The painting belongs to the Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark's national gallery in Copenhagen.

Storming of the Bastille - Jean-Pierre-L.title: The Storming of the Bastille (Prise de la Bastille)
facts: The painting records the storming of the Bastille prison-fortress on 14 July 1789, the event that ignited the French Revolution.
Houel painted it in watercolour and gouache rather than oil, working close to the time of the event itself.
The work is held by the Musee Carnavalet in Paris, the museum dedicated to the history of the city.
Houel was better known for documenting the landscapes and antiquities of Sicily and Malta during a long study journey there.

Study A - Amadeo de Souza Cardoso 1913.j.title: Study A
facts: The work belongs to the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon, which holds the largest collection of the artist's paintings.
1913 was the year the artist reached an international audience, showing eight pictures at New York's Armory Show.
Souza Cardoso refused to settle into a single label, moving freely between cubism, futurism, and expressionism.

Study for A Sunday on La Grande Jatte -.title: Study for A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
facts: Seurat made over 60 studies for the final Grande Jatte, hauling his canvas to the island every morning for months.
The finished painting took two years of dots; this oil sketch shows the looser hand he hid in the final work.
The island of La Grande Jatte sits in the Seine just west of Paris, a popular spot for Sunday strollers in Seurat's day.

Study for Improvisation 31 (Sea Battle).title: Study for Improvisation 31 (Sea Battle)
facts: This works out the idea for the larger painting, two sailing ships locked in combat on heaving waves.
The tall masts show up as thin black lines, and a white city seems to topple at the upper left.
Kandinsky drew the theme from the apocalyptic visions of the Bible's Book of Revelation.
Improvisation was his term for works made spontaneously, an unplanned expression of inner life.
Even the finished version stays half-hidden, its battle dissolving into washes of loose color.

Subway Escalator - Frank Hinder 1953.jpg.title: Subway Escalator
facts: The painting captures the speed and energy of the old wooden escalators at Sydney's Wynyard station, with commuters shown from several viewpoints at once.
Hinder built the composition using dynamic symmetry, a system of geometric proportion meant to express his belief in the interrelation of all things.
It was the last of a series of subway scenes Hinder worked on between 1929 and 1953, and is held by the Art Gallery of South Australia.
The medium is tempera and oil on canvas laid on composition board.

Summer Landscape - Venny Soldan-Brofeldt.title: Summer Landscape
facts: Soldan-Brofeldt was a pioneering Finnish woman artist who trained in Paris and was known for her vigorous, unsentimental realism.
She married the writer Juhani Aho, and their Helsinki home became a gathering place for figures like Jean Sibelius and Akseli Gallen-Kallela.
Beyond painting she worked as an illustrator, graphic artist, wood sculptor and jewelry designer.
Her two sons founded the photography and film company Aho and Soldan, and she later travelled as its representative.

Summer Night - Harald Sohlberg 1899.jpg.title: Summer Night
facts: Sohlberg painted this to celebrate his own engagement; the table set for two on the veranda marks the occasion.
There are no people in the scene, only the traces they left: half-empty glasses, a pair of gloves and a hat on the flower box.
It captures the lingering, luminous twilight of a Nordic summer night, when the sky never fully darkens.
Sohlberg is most famous for Winter Night in the Mountains, later voted Norway's national painting.

Summer's Day - Berthe Morisot 1879.jpg.title: Summer's Day
facts: Morisot painted two women in a rowboat on the lake in the Bois de Boulogne, a wooded park on the western edge of Paris.
Her quick zig-zag brushstrokes were especially suited to catching the flicker of light on moving water.
After the birth of her daughter Julie, daily walks in the Bois gave Morisot the urge to paint outdoors again.
She showed in nearly every Impressionist exhibition and was a central figure of the movement, not a fringe member.

Sun, Tower, Airplane (Soleil, Tour, Aero.title: Sun, Tower, Airplane (Soleil, Tour, Aéroplane)
facts: It packs three thrills of the new century into one canvas: the Eiffel Tower, a biplane in flight, and a giant Ferris wheel.
Everything radiates from a kaleidoscopic sun, the warm and cool colors spinning outward like a prism.
Delaunay painted it as a frank celebration of modern machines and speed, in the excited years just before the First World War.
The picture is nearly a perfect square, about four and a half feet on each side.

Sunrise over the Eastern Sea - Fujishima.title: Sunrise over the Eastern Sea
facts: Fujishima was a leader of yoga, the movement that brought Western oil-painting techniques into Japanese art around 1900.
He took up the sunrise theme after a 1928 commission to decorate the Showa Emperor's study, then chased dawns from northern Honshu to Taiwan.
The composition is stripped to almost nothing: a single sailboat against broad, clear planes of sea and sky.
The painting is held by the Artizon Museum in Tokyo.

Sunset at Éragny - Camille Pissarro 1890.title: Sunset at Éragny
facts: Éragny was Pissarro's final home - Monet lent him the money to buy the farmhouse whose meadows fill his late canvases.
Pissarro lived at Éragny from 1884 until his death in 1903, and it became the most painted subject of his later years.

Sunset in the Mediterranean from an Orie.title: Sunset in the Mediterranean from an Orient Steamer
facts: Goodwin, influenced by Turner and the Pre-Raphaelites, produced more than 800 atmospheric watercolors during a lifetime of world travel.
He inscribed the canvas 'Stromboli', the smoking Italian volcano island, recording exactly where at sea he caught this sunset.
The critic John Ruskin championed him and took him on a European tour where he sketched directly from nature.
His first painting was exhibited at the Royal Academy when he was only fifteen.

Surrealist Fusion - Eduardo Kobra 2025.j.title: Surrealist Fusion
facts: Kobra is a Brazilian muralist who has painted thousands of large-scale works across five continents.
His signature look builds figures from a kaleidoscope of brightly colored squares and triangles.
He often sets a realistic black-and-white portrait against those vivid geometric patterns for contrast.
He grew up in Sao Paulo and started out painting graffiti before turning to giant public murals.

Synchromy - Morgan Russell 1914.jpg.title: Synchromy
facts: Russell co-founded Synchromism, one of the first American abstract movements, which built compositions from color the way music is built from sound.
The word 'synchromy' means 'with color,' coined by Russell and Stanton Macdonald-Wright to set their work apart from the Cubists they knew in Paris.
Russell trained in part as a sculptor, and he spoke of his color forms as having weight and volume, like shapes turning in space.

Take Me To The Beach - Brooke Borcherdin.title: Take Me To The Beach
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 24 by 36 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

The Abduction of Europa - Rembrandt 1632.title: The Abduction of Europa
facts: The scene comes from Ovid's Metamorphoses, in which the god Zeus disguises himself as a gentle bull to carry the princess Europa across the sea.
In the myth, Europa is carried off to Crete, and the continent of Europe is traditionally said to take its name from her.
This is one of very few mythological subjects Rembrandt ever painted; he far preferred portraits and biblical scenes.
He worked it on a single oak panel rather than canvas, and the painting now hangs at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles.

The Beach at Fécamp - Gustave Loiseau 18.title: The Beach at Fécamp
facts: Loiseau, a baker's son who took up painting with an inheritance, became known for cross-hatched brushwork he called 'en treillis' - like lattice.
Fécamp is a fishing and former cod-trade port on the chalk-cliff coast of Normandy in northern France.
Loiseau spent summers painting the Normandy coast and the Seine, often returning to the same view in different weather and light.

The Bedroom - Vincent van Gogh October 1.title: The Bedroom
facts: This is the first of three versions; Van Gogh painted it of his own room in the Yellow House at Arles, where he hoped to host fellow artists.
He chose flat, bright colors on purpose, writing to his brother Theo that the picture was meant to suggest rest and calm to the eye.
The original canvas was damaged by damp while Van Gogh was in hospital, which is partly why he later painted two careful copies.
You can tell the versions apart by the small pictures on the right wall, which differ in each one.
This first version now hangs in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

The Beyond - Georgia O'Keeffe 1972.jpg.title: The Beyond
facts: A black band runs along the bottom while stacked blues fill the rest, split by a single thin white line like a far-off horizon.
This was O'Keeffe's last oil painting made without help, completed as failing eyesight forced her to stop painting on her own.
Macular degeneration had left her with only peripheral vision, yet she went on creating with assistants for years afterward.
The painting is held by the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe.

The Boulevard Montmartre on a Winter Mor.title: The Boulevard Montmartre on a Winter Morning
facts: One of fourteen views Pissarro painted of this boulevard from his hotel room over the winter and spring of 1897.
He painted the wide street in snow, rain, fog, and sun, at morning, afternoon, sunset, and night, from a single high window.
The high viewpoint and the long, receding sweep of the boulevard give the scene its simple, dramatic perspective.
This canvas is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

The Bridge at Villeneuve-la-Garenne - Al.title: The Bridge at Villeneuve-la-Garenne
facts: The cast-iron and stone bridge, built in 1844, linked a riverside village to the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis across the Seine.
New, modern bridges turn up again and again in Sisley's paintings of the 1870s as emblems of a changing France.
The dealer Paul Durand-Ruel bought it straight from Sisley in August 1872, just months after it was painted.
The painting now hangs at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

The Channel of Gravelines, Petit Fort Ph.title: The Channel of Gravelines, Petit Fort Philippe
facts: Seurat painted this in the summer of 1890 at the Channel port of Gravelines, his final season of work before he died.
It is one of four canvases of the harbor, possibly meant as a set marking different times of day.
He died in March 1891 at just 31, likely of diphtheria, only months after exhibiting these last seascapes.
The cool, near-empty quay shows how far Seurat carried his dot technique toward calm and stillness.

The Channel Sketchbook 13 - J. M. W. Tur.title: The Channel Sketchbook 13
facts: In his final years Turner filled sketchbooks with rapid coastal studies of the English Channel, reducing sea and sky to washes of pure atmosphere.
Turner left nearly 300 sketchbooks and thousands of works on paper to the British nation, a bequest now held mainly at Tate Britain.

The Channel Sketchbook 45 - J. M. W. Tur.title: The Channel Sketchbook 45
facts: One of Turner's late Channel studies, where sky and water blur into near-abstract veils of light.
Working in small sketchbooks let Turner capture fleeting weather and light at sea, studies he could later draw on for finished oils.

The Channel Sketchbook, page 29 - J.M.W..title: The Channel Sketchbook, Page 29
facts: From a pocket sketchbook Turner carried on Channel crossings in his last decade - sea and sky dissolved to almost pure color.
Turner left more than 30,000 sketches and watercolors to the British nation.
His vast studio bequest, the Turner Bequest, passed to the nation after his death in 1851 and is now largely held by Tate.

The Channel Sketchbook, page 48 - J.M.W..title: The Channel Sketchbook, Page 48
facts: These late watercolor pages were private experiments never meant for sale - closer to abstraction than anything publicly shown for another 60 years.
Turner crossed the English Channel repeatedly in his final years, sketching the changing light over open water from the deck.

The City of Paris - Robert Delaunay c. 1.title: The City of Paris
facts: This large canvas, now at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, was a centerpiece of the 1912 Salon des Independants.
At its heart stand the mythological Three Graces, lifted from classical art but rebuilt here from prismatic shards of color.
The Eiffel Tower rises from the abstracted cityscape, knitting ancient myth and modern Paris into one image.
Delaunay painted it at a turning point, moving away from Cubism toward the pure color abstraction that would define his career.

The City, No. 2 (La Ville no. 2) - Rober.title: The City, No. 2 (La Ville n° 2)
facts: It looks down on Paris from above, the Eiffel Tower a pale silhouette glimpsed through a curtained window at the back.
The whole scene is built from tiny squarish dabs, a mosaic-like touch Delaunay borrowed from the dot painter Georges Seurat.
It comes from a run of eight 'City' canvases he painted between 1909 and 1911, working out how to break a view into shifting planes.
He showed it at the 1911 Salon des Indépendants, the open Paris exhibition where new painters tested their boldest work.

The Coming Storm - Winslow Homer 1901.jp.title: The Coming Storm
facts: Homer spent his last decades in a studio on the Maine coast, painting the sea fifty feet from his door in every mood it offered.
He painted it in watercolor over graphite, a medium he handled with the speed needed to catch shifting weather.
From 1883 Homer lived at Prouts Neck in Scarborough, Maine, in a remodeled carriage house close above the surf.

The Dance Lesson - Edgar Degas c. 1879.j.title: The Dance Lesson
facts: This is the first of about forty ballet scenes Degas painted in the same unusually wide, narrow format, like a strip of film.
Degas cared less about the polished performance than the candid backstage moments, dancers resting, stretching, or waiting their turn.
It was shown at the Fifth Impressionist Exhibition in 1880, where it drew little notice at the time.
The painting now hangs at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

The Dogana and Santa Maria della Salute,.title: The Dogana and Santa Maria della Salute, Venice
facts: Turner visited Venice only three times but made it his signature subject, dissolving the city into light on water.
Critics mocked these late Venices as 'soapsuds and whitewash'; Monet and the Impressionists studied them like textbooks.
Turner exhibited this canvas at the Royal Academy in London in 1843, where it sold straight from the show.
The domed church is Santa Maria della Salute, built as Venice's thanks for the end of a 17th-century plague.

The Eclipse - Alma Thomas 1970.jpg.title: The Eclipse
facts: Thomas taught junior-high art in Washington for 35 years and began her abstract career in her seventies.
In 2015 she became the first Black woman to have a painting enter the White House collection.
The painting was the last work in her Space series, inspired by the total solar eclipse seen across the eastern United States on March 7, 1970.
A dark blue core ringed by bands of color sits off-center, suggesting the moon's slow passage across the sun.
It belongs to the Smithsonian American Art Museum, given by the artist in 1978, the year she died.

The Fall of Phaeton - Peter Paul Rubens.title: The Fall of Phaeton
facts: The myth tells of Phaeton, son of the sun god, who begged to drive the sun's chariot but lost control and scorched the earth.
To stop the runaway chariot, Zeus strikes Phaeton down with a thunderbolt, the dramatic moment Rubens chose to paint.
Rubens painted it during his formative years studying in Italy, where he absorbed the energy of Renaissance masters.
He kept the picture and reworked it years later; the painting now hangs at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

The Fighting Temeraire - J. M. W. Turner.title: The Fighting Temeraire
facts: The painting shows a tugboat towing the warship Temeraire up the Thames to a breaker's yard, where the veteran ship was scrapped in 1838.
The Temeraire had fought with distinction at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, more than thirty years before Turner painted her final voyage.
Turner sets the scene against a blazing sunset, casting the steam tug and the doomed sailing ship as the age of sail giving way to steam.
In a 2005 BBC poll the work was voted the nation's favourite painting in a British collection.
Turner refused to sell the picture during his lifetime, leaving it to the British nation; it hangs in the National Gallery in London.

The Forest Has Eyes - Bev Doolittle 1984.title: The Forest Has Eyes
facts: Fifteen faces are hidden in the woods: rocks and waterfalls that read as landscape up close resolve into watching Native American faces when seen from a distance.
A lone rider leads a pack horse through a shallow stream, unaware of the eyes that fill the forest around him.
The work became one of Doolittle's most famous images and the subject of a 1998 book pairing the painting with text by Elise Maclay.
It is a defining example of her camouflage technique, which rewards slow looking by revealing images the first glance misses.
Doolittle painted it in watercolor and it was issued as a signed, numbered limited edition by The Greenwich Workshop.

The Grand Canal, Venice - Claude Monet 1.title: The Grand Canal, Venice
facts: Monet took this view down the Grand Canal toward the domed church of Santa Maria della Salute, painting from a palazzo's boat landing.
It comes from his only trip to Venice, in 1908, when he made dozens of canvases of the city's light and water.
Monet cared less for Venice's famous monuments than for the play of light and reflection across its canals.
He began the pictures on the spot but finished many later in his Giverny studio from memory and notes.

The Great Wave off Kanagawa - Katsushika.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
facts: Hokusai was about 70 when he cut this design - he claimed nothing he made before 70 was worth counting.
It's a woodblock print, not a painting: thousands of impressions were sold cheaply, about the price of a bowl of noodles.
Mount Fuji, the real subject of the series, hides in the trough of the wave.
The print opens his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which actually runs to forty-six designs.
The deep blue came from Prussian blue, a then-new imported synthetic pigment that did not fade like older Japanese blues.

The Harbour at L'Estaque - Georges Braqu.title: The Harbour at L'Estaque
facts: L'Estaque is a small fishing port on the Mediterranean just outside Marseille, in the south of France.
Braque went there with his friend Othon Friesz and stayed from autumn 1906 into the winter, painting the harbor in hot, unmixed color.
He chose the spot on purpose because Cézanne had painted the same hills and water there decades earlier, and Braque wanted to follow his lead.
This is one of the few truly Fauvist pictures Braque made before he turned toward the broken planes that became Cubism.

The Harvest - Vincent van Gogh June 1888.title: The Harvest
facts: Van Gogh painted this view of the Crau plain near Arles in a single furious week of harvest weather and judged it his best landscape yet.
He wrote to Theo that the canvas 'kills all the rest' he had done that summer.
He built the scene from receding bands of fields, carts, and haystacks to draw the eye deep toward the blue hills.
It is a cornerstone of the Van Gogh Museum collection in Amsterdam.

The Houses of Parliament, Sunset - Claud.title: The Houses of Parliament, Sunset
facts: Monet painted Parliament from a terrace at St Thomas' Hospital, always at dusk, working on dozens of canvases at once as the light shifted.
He loved London's fog and said without it the city wouldn't be beautiful.
The Parliament views belong to a large London series Monet worked on across several winter stays in the city.
He started the canvases in London but reworked and finished many back at Giverny, refining the haze from memory.

The Hozu River - Takeuchi Seihō 1888.jpg.title: The Hozu River
facts: The Hozu is a river in Kyoto Prefecture famous for its gorge and traditional boat rides through the rapids.
Takeuchi Seiho painted it in ink and colour on silk, the classic materials of nihonga.
Seiho was one of the founders of modern nihonga and a master of the prewar Kyoto circle of painters.

The Japanese Footbridge - Claude Monet 1.title: The Japanese Footbridge
facts: Monet had the arched wooden bridge built over his Giverny water garden in 1895, inspired by the Japanese prints he collected.
He painted the bridge about a dozen times around 1899 and 1900, viewing it from different angles over the lily pond.
He dug the pond himself by diverting a branch of a nearby stream, designing the whole water garden as a living subject to paint.
When the bridge pictures were shown in 1900, critics noted at once how much they owed to Japanese art.

The Kitchen at Manhufe House - Amadeo de.title: The Kitchen at Manhufe House (Cozinha da Casa de Manhufe)
facts: The subject is the kitchen of the artist's own family home, the Casa de Manhufe in northern Portugal.
He painted it in oil on a small wood panel, roughly 29 by 50 centimeters.
The kitchen that inspired the picture still survives, looking much as it did in 1913.
The painting is held in the modern collection of the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon.

The Little Maure Mountains - Henri-Edmon.title: The Little Maure Mountains
facts: Cross moved to the wild Côte d'Azur for his health and painted it in blocks of violet and gold that pointed straight toward Fauvism - Matisse came to visit and learn.
The Massif des Maures is a low coastal mountain range in Provence, near Cross's home at Saint-Clair by Le Lavandou.
By this date Cross had loosened his strict dots into broad, mosaic-like brushmarks of saturated color.

The Little Mermaid Thinking of the Princ.title: The Little Mermaid Thinking of the Prince
facts: It illustrates Hans Christian Andersen's tale of the mermaid who longs for the human prince she has saved from the sea.
Iwasaki built her soft, glowing watercolors with blurring and shading borrowed from traditional Japanese ink painting.
She illustrated more than seventy children's books, devoting her art to the theme of peace and happiness for children.
Two museums in Japan, in Tokyo and Azumino, are dedicated entirely to her original picture-book art.

The Magpie - Claude Monet 1868.jpg.title: The Magpie
facts: A single magpie perched on a gate is the only living thing in this vast field of snow.
Monet painted it during an unusually heavy winter near Étretat on the Normandy coast.
It contains some of his earliest colored shadows - blue and violet rather than black - a hallmark the Impressionists would make their own.
The official Salon rejected it as too coarse; today it is one of the best-loved paintings at the Musée d'Orsay.

The Mellow Pad - Stuart Davis Helen Stua.title: The Mellow Pad
facts: Davis worked on this painting on and off for about six years, layering bold shapes to capture the energy of the jazz he loved.
He built it on top of the composition of an earlier 1931 work, 'House and Street,' reworking it into pure abstraction.
Davis called the finished canvas 'probably the most objective Art realization of my life.'
Its abstract, rhythmic layering anticipated the looser, less realistic painting of Abstract Expressionism.
The painting is held by the Brooklyn Museum in New York.

The Meuse Near Dordrecht (La Meuse près.title: The Meuse Near Dordrecht (La Meuse près de Dordrecht)
facts: Dordrecht is an old harbor city in the Netherlands, set where several rivers meet, long a favorite subject for painters of water and sky.
Luce based this view on a trip to the Netherlands the year before, sketching on the spot and finishing the canvas in his Paris studio.
By the late 1890s Luce had loosened his strict pointillism into a freer, brighter Impressionist handling of light, seen here on the river.
The painting is now held by the Indianapolis Museum of Art.

The Ninth Wave - Hovhannes Aivazovsky 18.title: The Ninth Wave
facts: The title comes from an old sailors' belief that waves build in a series and the ninth is the largest and most dangerous.
Survivors of a shipwreck cling to a mast at dawn, the warm light hinting they may yet live through the storm.
Aivazovsky painted the sea entirely from memory; his studio windows faced a courtyard, not the water.
Over a 60-year career he produced about 6,000 paintings, making him one of history's most prolific marine painters.
An Armenian from Crimea, he used his earnings to give his hometown of Feodosia a school, library, and art gallery.

The Old Guitarist - Pablo Picasso 1903.j.title: The Old Guitarist
facts: Picasso painted it in Barcelona when he was barely twenty and so poor he reportedly burned his own drawings to heat his cold studio.
X-rays and infrared scans found at least three other figures hidden underneath, including a young mother with a child.
A faint outline of one of those buried figures, a woman's face, can be seen near the guitarist's neck with the naked eye.
The stretched, bony pose reflects the influence of the old Spanish master El Greco, whom Picasso admired.
It hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago as part of the Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection.

The Palazzo Ducale - Claude Monet 1908.j.title: The Palazzo Ducale
facts: From Monet's only trip to Venice, at age 68 - he called the city 'too beautiful to paint' and then made 37 canvases.
The subject is the Doge's Palace, the pink-and-white Gothic seat of Venice's rulers, seen across the lagoon.
Monet painted the palace as a shimmering wall of color reflected in moving water, more light than architecture.
He worked the Venice canvases for years afterward in Giverny before showing them in Paris in 1912.

The Persistence of Memory - Salvador Dal.title: The Persistence of Memory
facts: It is tiny: about 9.5 by 13 inches, smaller than a sheet of paper, packed with sharp detail meant to be studied up close.
When people asked if the soft watches came from Einstein's theory of relativity, Dalí said no; he was thinking of Camembert cheese melting in the sun.
The pale shape draped across the center, eyelashes closed, is a soft self-portrait of Dalí's own profile.
The orange watch at the lower left does not melt; instead it is swarming with ants, a sign of decay Dalí used often.
An anonymous donor gave the painting to New York's Museum of Modern Art in 1934, and it has stayed there ever since.

The Quai Saint-Michel and Notre-Dame - M.title: The Quai Saint-Michel and Notre-Dame
facts: This was one of about ten views Luce painted of Notre-Dame de Paris, here glowing in warm oranges, pinks and reds against bluish shadows.
He filled the quay with ordinary Parisians: well-dressed strollers, servants carrying produce, a grandmother with a child, a baker's boy balancing his basket on his head.
The Musee d'Orsay, which holds the painting, notes it marks Luce's shift from his Neo-Impressionist years toward a later, more populist phase.
The cathedral rises from finely juxtaposed brushstrokes, while broader strokes carry the bridge and embankment below.

The Rise of the Green Square and the Vio.title: The Rise of the Green Square and the Violin Woman
facts: Around 1915 and 1916 the artist grew close to Sonia and Robert Delaunay, who had taken refuge in Portugal during the war.
He was active in Orpheu, the circle of writers and artists that launched Portuguese modernism in those years.
In 1916 he mounted a large solo show of more than a hundred works in Porto, later carried to Lisbon.

The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak - Alb.title: The Rocky Mountains, Lander's Peak
facts: The view is based on sketches Bierstadt made in 1859 while travelling with Frederick Lander's government survey expedition through the Wyoming Range.
An encampment of Native Americans fills the foreground beneath the towering peak Bierstadt named for the survey's leader.
It was the first of his works promoted with a single-picture exhibition, complete with pamphlets, engravings and a touring show.
In 1865 a British railway entrepreneur paid 25,000 dollars for it, then the highest price ever for an American painting.
The canvas now hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

The Sawmill, December Sun - Ester Almqvi.title: The Sawmill, December Sun
facts: One of Sweden's pioneering women modernists; her drawing 'The Meeting' was chosen for the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights stamp.
Her mature work shows a strong kinship with van Gogh in its fiery, intense brushwork.
She willed her paintings to the Malmo Art Museum, where this canvas is now held.
Wide recognition came only after her death in 1934.

The Sea at Camaret, The Red Rocks - Maxi.title: The Sea at Camaret, The Red Rocks
facts: Camaret is a fishing port at the far western tip of Brittany, on the Crozon peninsula reaching into the Atlantic.
The scene reflects Luce's love of unspoiled nature, here the rugged red rocks and open sea of the Breton coast.
Luce worked the divisionist method by laying separate strokes of pure color side by side rather than blending them on the canvas.
A nineteenth-century sardine port, Camaret later turned to lobster fishing in the twentieth century.

The Season of Now - Brooke Borcherding.j.title: The Season of Now
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 18 by 24 inches, painted plein air on location.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

The Seine - Henry Ossawa Tanner c. 1902..title: The Seine
facts: Tanner left American racism for Paris, where he became the first African American painter with international acclaim.
This quiet river view hangs in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.
Tanner was the son of a bishop in the African Methodist Episcopal Church and studied under the realist Thomas Eakins in Philadelphia.
In 1923 the French government named him a chevalier of the Legion of Honor, a rare distinction for a foreign artist.

The Seine at Giverny - Claude Monet 1897.title: The Seine at Giverny
facts: For his 'Mornings on the Seine' series Monet rose at 3:30am and rowed out to anchor before first light, painting the same bend day after day.
He kept a rack of canvases on his boat, moving from one to the next as the dawn light changed minute by minute.
The series captures the river near Giverny wrapped in soft mist, water and trees blurring into mirrored reflections.
He showed the morning pictures together in 1898, presenting them as a single sustained study of one stretch of river.

The Sentinel - Bev Doolittle 1991.jpg.title: The Sentinel
facts: A wolf is hidden in plain sight: both the watching brave and the land itself wear a wolf headdress, binding human and earth together.
A double rainbow, mirrored in its own reflection, arcs across the scene to form a complete circle framing the composition.
The mood came from a memory of an evening walk on the Crow Reservation in Montana, when sun broke under rain clouds to make a golden sunset.
The wolf appears as a guardian spirit, echoing the painting's theme of watchfulness and shared responsibility in nature.
It was published in April 1991 in a limited edition of 35,000 signed and numbered prints by The Greenwich Workshop.

The Sky - Vicente do Rego Monteiro 1962..title: The Sky
facts: Rego Monteiro was a key figure in Sao Paulo's 1922 Modern Art Week, the event that launched modernism in Brazil.
Trained in Paris from age twelve, he exhibited at the Salon des Independants in 1913 as a teenager.
His distinctive style merged Cubism and Art Deco with the geometry of ancient Marajoara pottery from the Amazon.
A studio fire in the late 1920s destroyed many of his finest works, contributing to his long obscurity at home.
He was also a published poet, and Brazil only rediscovered his art in the mid-1960s.

The sloop - Amadeo de Souza Cardoso c. 1.title: The Sloop (A Chalupa)
facts: The painting is signed in the lower right corner in the artist's stacked hand, 'amadeo / de souza / cardoso'.
It is held in the Centro de Arte Moderna of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation in Lisbon.
Souza Cardoso belonged to the first generation of Portuguese modernist painters and was in dialogue with the European avant-garde.

The Son of Man - René Magritte 1946.jpg.title: The Son of Man
facts: Magritte painted it as a self-portrait, then sold it to his friend and lawyer Harry Torczyner in 1964.
Look closely and one of the man's eyes peeks out past the edge of the floating apple.
Magritte said the work is about how everything we see hides something else, and how we always want to see what is hidden.
The bowler hat appears again and again across Magritte's paintings; he was fond of the ordinary, anonymous hat.
He finished it three years before his death in 1967, and it became his most famous image.

The Starry Night - Vincent van Gogh June.title: The Starry Night
facts: Painted from his asylum room at Saint-Rémy - but from memory and imagination, since he wasn't allowed to paint in his bedroom.
The village is invented; the cypress and swirling sky came from his head, not the window.
Van Gogh considered it a failure and sold not one painting like it in his lifetime.
It has hung at the Museum of Modern Art in New York since 1941 and is now one of the most recognized paintings in the world.
The tall dark cypress in front was a tree he linked with graveyards and the passage of time.

The Three Windows, the Tower and the Whe.title: The Three Windows, the Tower and the Wheel
facts: The tower is the Eiffel Tower and the wheel is a giant Ferris wheel, both melting into a grid of colored panes.
Delaunay turned the old idea of a painting as a window onto the world inside out, making the act of seeing color itself the real subject.
It belongs to his 'Windows' series, painted across 1912, that pushed him to the edge of pure abstraction.
The poet Guillaume Apollinaire coined the word 'Orphism' for this kind of color painting and wrote a poem, also called 'Windows,' alongside the series.
The canvas is wide and low, stretching well over six feet across.

The Tugboat, Canal in Samois - Paul Sign.title: The Tugboat, Canal in Samois
facts: By 1901 Signac's dots had widened into small bricks of color - he compared the method to mosaics he'd admired in Venice.
Samois-sur-Seine is a riverside village southeast of Paris, near the Fontainebleau forest, on a quiet bend of the Seine.
Signac usually painted such river scenes in the studio from on-the-spot sketches, reworking nature into ordered grids of color.

The Water Lilies - The Clouds - Claude M.title: The Water Lilies - The Clouds
facts: This is one of the enormous wall-sized panels Monet made for the oval rooms of the Musée de l'Orangerie in Paris.
The pond's surface reflects only clouds and sky, so the viewer seems to look down and up at once.
Monet worked on these grand decorations from about 1914 until his death in 1926, repainting them for years.
He gave the panels to France as a gift, conceiving them as a calm, immersive space that wraps around the viewer.
By this stage cataracts were clouding his sight, yet he pressed on with the largest project of his life.

The Water Lily Pond in the Evening - Cla.title: The Water Lily Pond in the Evening
facts: Monet dug the pond himself at Giverny and diverted a river branch to feed it, then painted it for thirty years.
Painted while cataracts dimmed his sight - the late pond pictures burn with oranges and purples he partly saw and partly remembered.
In these late works the pond fills the whole canvas, with no bank or horizon, just floating lilies and reflected light.
The water lily became the central obsession of Monet's final decades, the subject of hundreds of canvases.

The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede - Rui.title: The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede
facts: Ruisdael gathers the classic Dutch elements here: low land, wide water and a vast sky, all converging on the towering mill.
Look closely and the miller stands on the mill's gallery, seeming to study the weather in the gathering clouds.
The painting hangs in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum on loan from the Amsterdam Museum.
It became so beloved that copyists in the Rijksmuseum reproduced it more often than any other painting in the galleries.
The actual mill is long gone, though its foundations survive; a different nearby mill is often mistaken for it today.

the_artist_s_garden_in_argenteuil_a_corn.title: The Artist's Garden in Argenteuil (A Corner of the Garden with Dahlias)
facts: Monet's house at Argenteuil was a gathering place for the Impressionists, drawing Renoir, Manet, Sisley, and Caillebotte to paint together.
The dealer Paul Durand-Ruel bought the picture straight from Monet in December 1873, early support that helped keep the painter afloat.
Bright clumps of dahlias nearly swallow a strolling couple, the flowers given as much weight as the figures.
Argenteuil's gardens and riverbanks gave Monet some of his sunniest, most carefree subjects of the early 1870s.

Thomson No. 3 (Sunset Bay) - Douglas Cou.title: Thomson No. 3 (Sunset Bay)
facts: Coupland took a low-quality digital copy of a Tom Thomson landscape found online and used Photoshop to flatten it into blocks of solid colour.
He called such works 'secret handshakes': abstractions to outsiders, but instantly recognizable as Canadian icons to Canadians.
The series reworks Tom Thomson and the Group of Seven, the painters who shaped Canada's national image of its wilderness.
Coupland is also a bestselling novelist whose 1991 book 'Generation X' gave a name to a generation.

Tiptoe Through the Tulips - Alma Thomas.title: Tiptoe Through the Tulips
facts: The title echoes the song made famous in 1968 by the ukulele-playing singer Tiny Tim.
Thomas painted vertical stripes from small dabs of color, the mosaic-like style sometimes called her Alma stripes.
The work entered the National Gallery of Art in Washington, where it remains in the collection.
Thomas drew her flower subjects from nature, including the rows of tulips familiar from gardens and postcards.
She developed this signature abstract style only after retiring from teaching, late in her seventies.

Tram kaleidoscope - Frank Hinder 1948.jp.title: Tram Kaleidoscope
facts: Hinder fragments a Sydney tram and the street around it into simultaneous views, blending Cubism, Futurism, and Orphism into one busy composition.
The cylindrical tram, distant buildings, a passing car, and a crowd of commuters are unified by a repetition of forms running through the picture.
Hinder had finished the conception by 1939, but wartime service in the camouflage unit delayed the large painting until 1948.
The painting is held by the Art Gallery of New South Wales.

Transition - Brooke Borcherding.jpg.title: Transition
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 24 by 24 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Two Breton Women in a Meadow - Émile Ber.title: Two Breton Women in a Meadow
facts: Bernard was barely 20 when he developed Cloisonnism - flat color inside bold outlines, named after enamel work.
He traded paintings with Gauguin at Pont-Aven, and van Gogh kept this canvas's sister work in his collection.
Gauguin saw this style and adopted it for his breakthrough work, Vision of the Sermon, the same year.
Bernard painted it in Brittany, where local women still wore distinctive starched white headdresses and traditional dress.
Van Gogh admired the picture so much he made his own painted copy of it from memory.

Two Indian Horses - Bev Doolittle 1985.j.title: Two Indian Horses
facts: Two members of the Blackfeet Nation are camouflaged among a column of resting cavalry horses on the far left, easy to miss at first glance.
Doolittle turned most of the horses to look rightward on purpose, pulling the viewer's eye away from the hidden figures to delay the discovery.
The scene is set in the fall of 1875, with a Second Cavalry patrol resting its mounts on a ride from Fort Ellis, Montana.
Doolittle wanted viewers to see the horses and soldier first and only later realize what the hidden Blackfeet are doing.
It was published in 1985 by The Greenwich Workshop and later prompted a companion work, 'Two More Indian Horses.'

Under the Orange Tree - Berthe Morisot 1.title: Under the Orange Tree (Sous l'oranger)
facts: The girl is Morisot's daughter Julie, her favorite subject in the last two decades of the artist's life.
Julie sits in the garden of the family's winter home in the south of France, with her pet green parrot caged nearby.
Morisot was the leading woman of the Impressionist circle and exhibited in all but one of its group shows.

Une fenêtre (A Window) - Robert Delaunay.title: Une fenêtre (A Window)
facts: Delaunay's 'Windows' series broke the view into prisms of overlapping color; the poet Apollinaire coined the term 'Orphism' for this lyrical, music-like abstraction.
The Windows were painted in 1912 in rapid succession, twenty-two canvases finished in a single year between April and December.
Delaunay treated the windowpane as a surface that reflects and refracts light, dissolving the solid city into shifting planes of color.
He worked closely with his wife, the artist Sonia Delaunay, who shared his pursuit of what they called simultaneous color.

Untitled - Alma Thomas 1971.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: Thomas taught art in Washington public schools for 35 years before turning to full-time painting in retirement.
She built her abstractions from short, repeated dabs of color laid down like mosaic tiles.
Even her loosest works on paper began with planning, often guided by free-hand pencil marks on the surface.

Untitled - Alma Thomas 1973.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: Thomas's rhythmic color daubs were inspired by watching wind move through the holly tree outside her Washington window.
She painted her most celebrated work in her 80s, arthritis and all, steadying one arm with the other.
She taught art in Washington public schools for 35 years before devoting herself fully to painting in retirement.
Her signature surface is built from many small, tile-like strokes of color, a method known as her Alma stripes.

Untitled - Amadeo de Souza Cardoso c. 19.title: Untitled
facts: The artist died in October 1918 at age 30, one of the millions of victims of the global influenza pandemic.
His late work pushed toward bold color and near-abstraction, drawing on cubism, futurism, and the Delaunays' Orphism.
After decades of relative obscurity, he is now regarded as the most important Portuguese modernist painter.

Untitled - Frank Hinder 1945.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: Hinder was a leading figure in the Sydney modernist circle of the 1930s and 40s alongside Grace Crowley, Rah Fizelle, and Ralph Balson.
During the war he served as a camouflage officer, devising ways to conceal and disguise military and civilian sites from the air.

Untitled - José Dominguez Alvarez.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: Born in Porto to Galician parents, Alvarez painted brooding townscapes of houses, churches and castles under stormy skies and a stubborn golden light.
He was a founding member of the modernist group +Alem in Porto, which pushed back against the academic, naturalistic teaching of the day.
His melancholy, slightly distorted scenes drew on Spanish painters he admired, above all the elongated forms of El Greco.
His career was cut short when he died of tuberculosis in 1942, at only thirty-six.

Untitled - Joseph Stella 1914-1918.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: These years were Stella's most experimental, when he pushed the dynamism and electric light of New York toward full abstraction.
Born in the Italian village of Muro Lucano, Stella sailed for New York in 1896 and became a leading American modernist.
His Futurist visits to Paris and Italy taught him to render speed, machinery, and light as splintered, kinetic color.

Untitled - Lee Krasner 1946.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: From Krasner's 'Little Image' period, painted at a table in a small bedroom studio while Pollock worked in the barn.
Critics long filed her under 'Pollock's wife'; retrospectives since the 1980s placed her among the movement's founders.
The tightly woven 'Little Image' canvases packed small, repeated marks edge to edge across the surface.
Krasner had trained for years in figurative drawing and was an unusually rigorous, self-critical painter who often destroyed or reworked her own canvases.

Untitled - Robert Delaunay.jpg.title: Untitled
facts: Delaunay co-founded Orphism, an early abstract movement that pushed Cubism toward bright color and rhythmic, near-musical compositions.
He and his wife Sonia Delaunay built their art around 'simultaneous contrast,' the way adjacent colors intensify one another to the eye.

Untitled - Yellow - Ian Davenport 1994-1.title: Untitled (Yellow)
facts: Davenport's early-1990s work used a limited palette of household gloss paint poured to flow down the canvas and settle by gravity.
His preferred glossy paint gives a mirror-like finish, so viewers catch their own reflection in the surface.
He was the youngest artist ever shortlisted for the Turner Prize, nominated in 1991 at age 25.
Davenport emerged from the Young British Artists, having studied at Goldsmiths and shown in Damien Hirst's 1988 'Freeze' exhibition.

Untitled (36x36) - Brooke Borcherding 20.title: Untitled (36x36)
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 36 by 36 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Untitled (Textile design no. IV) - Franc.title: Untitled (Textile design no. IV)
facts: In the mid-1920s Hodgkins designed printed textiles for a Manchester firm; a leading New Zealand-born modernist, she spent most of her career in Britain.
She designed fabrics for the Calico Printers' Association from 1925, but chafed at the routine, comparing the steady job to being a racehorse shut in a stable.
In 1929 she joined the progressive Seven and Five Society, exhibiting alongside Ben Nicholson, Barbara Hepworth and Henry Moore.

Untitled #21 - Howardena Pindell 1978.jp.title: Untitled #21
facts: Pindell built shimmering surfaces from thousands of hand-punched paper dots, sometimes numbering each one.
She spent 12 years as a MoMA curator while making her own art at night.
Her method was process-based: she punched holes through stacked manila folders, then layered the leftover paper discs onto gridded canvases.
She often added glitter, thread, talcum powder, and even perfume so the works engaged more than just the eyes.

Urban Morning - Brooke Borcherding.jpg.title: Urban Morning
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 36 by 48 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Valley of the Yosemite - Albert Bierstad.title: Valley of the Yosemite
facts: Bierstadt visited Yosemite in 1863 with the writer Fitz Hugh Ludlow, who declared the valley surpassed the Alps in waterfalls and the Himalayas in cliffs.
Bierstadt wrote to a friend that on the trip he had found the Garden of Eden.
He deliberately left out any sign of people, showing a lake and a herd of deer to present Yosemite as raw, untouched nature.
Though grand in subject, it is a small painting in oil on paperboard, under half a metre wide.
It is held by the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

Venice - Henri-Edmond Cross c. 1903.jpg.title: Venice
facts: Cross anglicized his name from Delacroix to avoid comparison with the famous Romantic painter.
On a 1903 trip to Venice he gained new fluidity in watercolor; this sheet is watercolor over black chalk.
He carried the city's light home to Saint-Clair, working it up into several larger Venetian compositions.
Cross was born Henri-Edmond-Joseph Delacroix; 'croix' is French for cross, so his new name simply translated his old one.

Venice, from the Porch of Madonna della.title: Venice, from the Porch of Madonna della Salute
facts: The view is an imagined Venice rather than a faithful one, with the palaces dissolving into the lagoon through delicate reflections.
Turner built the composition from a slight pencil sketch made on his first Venice visit in 1819, worked up after his second trip in 1833.
The painting was shown at the Royal Academy exhibition of 1835 in London.
It was later bequeathed to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York by railroad magnate Cornelius Vanderbilt.

View from the Artist's Window - Martinus.title: View from the Artist's Window
facts: Rørbye painted the view from the drawing room of his childhood home on Amaliegade in Copenhagen, which he was about to leave.
The window frames a tension the period prized: the familiar room within and the harbor and distant horizon beyond.
He was studying under Christoffer Eckersberg, the painter regarded as the father of Danish Golden Age art.
The small canvas is now one of the highlights of the Danish Golden Age collection at the Statens Museum for Kunst.

View of a Valley in Normandy - Paul Huet.title: View of a Valley in Normandy
facts: Huet painted outdoors a generation before the Impressionists, helping free French landscape from the studio.
His 1833 Salon success earned him the nickname 'the Delacroix of landscape' among French critics.
He absorbed the loose, weather-filled skies of English painters John Constable and Richard Parkes Bonington.
From 1825 Huet worked often in Normandy, whose damp valleys and open coast became a recurring subject.

View of Bazincourt, Sunset - Camille Pis.title: View of Bazincourt, Sunset
facts: An eye ailment forced Pissarro to give up painting outdoors in bad weather - many late landscapes were painted through a window, including views toward Bazincourt.
Bazincourt-sur-Epte is the village beside Éragny, and its church tower recurs on the horizon of Pissarro's late landscapes.

View of Dresden by Moonlight - Johan Chr.title: View of Dresden by Moonlight
facts: The Norwegian-born Dahl settled in Dresden and shared a house with Caspar David Friedrich, the leading German Romantic painter.
Across the moonlit Elbe rise the silhouettes of the Frauenkirche, the cathedral and the Augustus Bridge.
Dahl is widely regarded as the father of Norwegian landscape painting.
The painting entered the Galerie Neue Meister in Dresden, where it still hangs.

View of Istanbul - Félix Ziem c. 1870s.j.title: View of Istanbul
facts: Ziem returned obsessively to Istanbul and Venice, painting golden harbors so popular he became one of the era's wealthiest artists.
He was the first living artist to have a work bought by the Louvre.
Critics often compared his luminous, light-soaked harbor scenes to the work of the English painter J. M. W. Turner.
He was associated with the Barbizon School and pitched a gypsy caravan there to paint the landscape outdoors.
A tireless traveler, Ziem journeyed to Constantinople, Cairo, Beirut, Algiers and Russia in search of subjects.

View of the Seine at Herblay - Paul Sign.title: View of the Seine at Herblay
facts: Painted the summer Signac anchored his boat at Herblay - the calm horizontal dots make the river feel like held breath.
Herblay is a town on the Seine northwest of Paris, where the river loops in broad bends through the Val-d'Oise countryside.
Signac saw a painting as a planned harmony of color and line, an idea he later set down in his influential 1899 book on Neo-Impressionism.

View of Warsaw from the Terrace of the R.title: View of Warsaw from the Terrace of the Royal Castle
facts: After Warsaw was nearly destroyed in World War II, Bellotto's exact city views guided the postwar rebuilding of many of its buildings.
Bellotto was the nephew and pupil of Canaletto and adopted his famous uncle's name while working abroad.
He served as court painter to Stanislaus II, the last king of Poland, and recorded daily life on the castle terrace.
The scene looks south along the Vistula toward the distant royal residence at Wilanów.
Bellotto built a career on precise vedute of European capitals, including Dresden, Vienna and Turin.

View of Zoutelande on the Island of Walc.title: View of Zoutelande on the Island of Walcheren
facts: Hart Nibbrig fell for the dune village of Zoutelande on first sight in 1910 and bought land there within a month.
He studied in Paris, where the dotted Neo-Impressionism of Camille and Lucien Pissarro reshaped how he painted.
Unlike strict French Pointillists, he loosened the technique, mixing fine dots with looser strokes to catch sparkling sunlight.
Zoutelande sits on Walcheren, a Dutch peninsula whose wide beaches and dunes draw painters for their unusually bright light.

View on the Grand Canal at San Geremia V.title: View on the Grand Canal at San Geremia, Venice
facts: Guardi learned from Canaletto but painted Venice more loosely, with flickering brushwork and a hazy, dreamlike light.
His Venetian views sold mainly to foreign visitors on the Grand Tour as souvenirs of the city.
Little celebrated in his own lifetime, Guardi was rediscovered when later Romantic taste embraced his atmospheric style.
The painting shows the mouth of the Cannaregio canal, with the church of San Geremia under reconstruction at left.
This work is held by the Frick Art Museum in Pittsburgh.

Vuelo - Leonardo Nierman 1974.jpg.title: Vuelo
facts: The Spanish title means 'flight,' and birds in motion were a recurring subject in Nierman's swirling abstractions.
A trained violinist, Nierman turned to painting after concluding he lacked the talent for a music career, and said music drove his sense of movement.
He earned a degree in business administration from Mexico's national university before dedicating himself to art.
His brilliant, flame-like color and dynamic forms led admirers to call him Mexico's Jackson Pollock.
He worked as a sculptor and muralist as well as a painter and showed internationally for decades.

Waiting For Lunch - Brooke Borcherding.j.title: Waiting For Lunch
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 24 by 30 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Wallingford Views - Brooke Borcherding.j.title: Wallingford Views
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 24 by 30 inches, painted plein air on location.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

Weymouth - J.M.W. Turner c. 1811.jpg.title: Weymouth
facts: Turner toured the Dorset coast for an engraving series, sketching fishing towns from cliff paths in all weathers.
The 1811 tour fed his Picturesque Views on the Southern Coast of England, a set of coastal scenes sold to subscribers as engravings.
His on-the-spot Weymouth sketches were worked up into a finished watercolor now at the Yale Center for British Art.

Wheat Field with Cypresses - Vincent van.title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
facts: Painted near the Saint-Rémy asylum the same summer as The Starry Night - the cypress was, he wrote, 'as beautiful as an Egyptian obelisk'.
He liked the composition so much he painted three versions, one as a gift for his mother and sister.
Thick, curling brushstrokes set the clouds, wheat, and trees all in motion across the canvas.
The Alpilles mountains behind the field appear in many of his paintings made during the asylum year.

Wheat Fields with Reaper Auvers - Vincen.title: Wheat Fields with Reaper, Auvers
facts: Painted at Auvers-sur-Oise in the last weeks of van Gogh's life, where he produced dozens of canvases at a rapid pace.
For van Gogh wheat stood for the cycle of life, and a reaper at work could carry the quiet idea of harvest and endings.
Auvers, a village near Paris, was his final home, chosen so he could be close to a doctor and to his brother Theo.

Wheatfield - Claude Monet 1881.jpg.title: Wheatfield
facts: A decade before the grainstack series, Monet was already drawn to wheat - here as a whole shimmering field under summer wind.
It dates to Monet's years at Vétheuil on the Seine, before he settled at Giverny.
Monet built the picture from countless small strokes, letting the eye blend them into ripening grain and moving air.

Wheatfield under Thunderclouds - Vincent.title: Wheatfield under Thunderclouds
facts: From his final weeks at Auvers, painted on an unusual double-square canvas - he said these wheat fields expressed 'sadness, extreme loneliness' but also health and strength.
The wide, panoramic shape gave him room for sweeping bands of green field beneath a heavy, stormy sky.
It is one of a group of large double-square landscapes he made at Auvers and now hangs at the Van Gogh Museum.

Whidbey Wood 2 - Brooke Borcherding.jpg.title: Whidbey Wood 2
facts: Acrylic on canvas, 22 by 28 inches.
Borcherding is a Seattle painter who calls her fractured, mosaic-like style 'deconstruction': scenes rebuilt from stacked squares of color.

White Daisies Rhapsody - Alma Thomas 197.title: White Daisies Rhapsody
facts: Dabs of white paint dance in a mosaic pattern over a springtime ground of citron and aquamarine.
The painting is held by the Smithsonian American Art Museum, which holds the largest public collection of her work.
Thomas drew her color and rhythm from flowers and gardens, a lifelong source for her abstractions.
She built the surface from short, repeated strokes laid down like tiles, the style known as her Alma stripes.

Winter Shadows - Alma Thomas c. 1960.jpg.title: Winter Shadows
facts: A transitional work from the years Thomas was moving from representation toward the pure color abstraction of her famous late style.
It is a watercolor in brush and black ink on paper, not one of her large color canvases.
The work is held by the National Gallery of Art in Washington as part of its Corcoran Collection.
Thomas arrived at her signature abstract style only around 1960, after retiring from a long career teaching art.

Woman with a Parasol in a Garden - Pierr.title: Woman with a Parasol in a Garden
facts: Renoir painted this in the large garden of a studio he rented in Montmartre, dabbing flowers and shrubs in flecks of pure color.
The man bends as if to pick a flower beside the woman, a small gesture hinting at the intimacy between the two figures.
It may be the garden picture admired by critics at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877.

Woodland Encounter - Bev Doolittle 1981..title: Woodland Encounter
facts: Doolittle calls this a study in camouflage by misdirection: a single bright fox placed dead center pulls the eye away from the rest of the busy snowscape.
Hidden in the surrounding woods are Native American riders on horseback, blended into the trees and snow.
She used the dense pattern of the winter trees to deliberately break the traditional rules about how space is composed in a painting.
The work is an early, key example of the camouflage approach that became Doolittle's signature.
It was painted in watercolor and published as a limited-edition print by The Greenwich Workshop.

Yellow-Red-Blue - Wassily Kandinsky 1925.title: Yellow-Red-Blue
facts: The title names the three primary colors, the building blocks Kandinsky taught in his Bauhaus classes.
The lighter, squared-off left side and the darker, looser right side set up a deliberate tension across the canvas.
It is often called the key work of his Bauhaus years and opens his so-called circle period.
Kandinsky paired colors with shapes and feelings, reading the circle as calm and the triangle as energy.
It hangs at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, which holds a major collection of his work.
